1. THE BEGINNING OF THE FIRST BOOK, STARTING FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE CREATION OF THE WORLD.
God is a Nature that lacks nothing, sufficient unto Himself for glory and for knowledge, neither needing glory from others nor comprehensible by another—unless one were to say that what is comprehensible about Him is His infinity and His incomprehensibility. And when I say God I mean Father and Son and Holy Spirit, which is the Godhead, according to the great father and theologian Gregory. The Divine, being thus, first gives substance to the angelic powers and the heavenly ministers and singers of the splendor above—not as needing them, but so that He might not be moved by the contemplation of Himself alone, but that the good might be poured out and make its way, and the benefaction extend to more; for this was the mark of the highest goodness. Then He also brings into being this material and visible world. And in the beginning He made the heaven and the earth. And while the earth was hidden in invisibility, since there was also darkness, and water lay upon its surface, God brought forth the light. And He separated the light and the darkness, and the light He called day, and the darkness He named night; to the beginning of the latter He gave the name evening, and to the first shining of the day the name morning. And there was evening, and there was morning, one day.
Now I know that it is written in the Lesser Genesis that on the first day the heavenly powers too were given substance before the rest by the Maker of all things; but since this Lesser Genesis is not numbered among the books of Hebrew wisdom approved by the divine fathers, I reckon nothing of what is written in it to be certain, nor do I assent to its account.
Then He established the firmament, stretching it out in the midst of the waters, so that the waters above it were held off, while those below were poured around the earth. It was called the firmament because its body is solid and does not have a thin or rarefied nature like the waters out of which it took its composition; and this was also named heaven. These things came to pass on the second day. On the third, God commanded the water that covered the whole face of the earth to be gathered together, and the dry land to appear. And the word became deed, and deep hollows came to be and received the waters. And the dry land He named earth, and the gatherings of the waters He named seas. On this same day plants and seeds were sent up from the earth; for it was needful that the earth, being unadorned, should be adorned with grasses and the countless growing things and the flowers and fruits of every kind and the graces of the trees. The fourth day had the coming-to-be of the luminaries, the sun and the moon and the rest of the stars. With these the Maker made the heaven resplendent, and He placed in these luminaries the light that had been brought forth on the first day, ordaining for them their motions and risings and courses and settings, so that through them the region of the earth might be lit and time might be numbered by their risings and settings, and so that they might furnish signs through these to those who attend most rightly to their shinings—and not to those who scrutinize them too curiously, or who, as one might say (to put it exactly), foolishly imagine that all our affairs are carried along together with the motion of the heavenly bodies. On the fifth of the days, again, when God commanded, the waters sent up the creeping things of living souls and the birds; of which some dwell in the waters and swim in them, while the birds cleave the air, creeping, as it were, aloft through it. On the sixth, the earth was commanded to bring forth the living soul—four-footed beasts and creeping things and wild animals—and according to the divine command all of these were brought forth. Now Scripture states that the earth was commanded to make the bringing-forth of the living soul, so that in this way it might show the difference of the soul of man from it. For the soul of the other living creatures grew up from the earth according to the command, and being earthy might reasonably be reckoned also perishable, since elsewhere too the Scripture says, "the soul of every beast is its

2. blood," and blood is in every way perishable. But the soul of man the earth did not send up; rather, the Divine put it into Adam as an in-breathing; and for this reason it is believed to be something divine and immortal.

The sixth of the days had also the man, fashioned by the hand of God. For the supreme Artist, having first established all things and brought forth the world in order and rhythm—wherefore it is also named "cosmos"—and having prepared it beforehand as a palace for the reception of a king, then brings forth the man himself, as a kind of king over the things on earth, ruled from above; and Him He did not establish by a mere command, but fashioned with His hands, making his creation not like that of the others, but distinct and incomparable. For all the rest were brought forth by a word, but man was deemed worthy of God's own handiwork. For "having taken dust from the earth," the book of Genesis says, "God formed the man, and breathed into him a living soul," through which man is also said to have come to be in the image of God. For certain of the things that belong essentially to the divine Nature are imaged in the soul of man—not present in it by nature, but by grace. For by nature the Divine is invisible and immortal, incomprehensible and incorruptible; and these belong to the soul too by grace, not by nature, for neither is its nature and substance comprehensible nor indeed visible, and it is incorruptible and immortal. And other distinguishing marks of the divine Nature have been observed in the soul by grace. The one fashioned He named Adam, which in the Hebrew tongue means "red," as Josephus says, because he had been fashioned out of red earth; for such is the virgin earth. Having thus brought forth the world in six days, on the seventh He rested; wherefore among the Hebrews the seventh of the days is held to be a day without work, whence it is also called the Sabbath; and "Sabbath" in the tongue of the Hebrews means "rest."

And God placed Adam in the paradise that He Himself had planted, where there was the tree of life and the tree of knowledge—or, according to Josephus, of understanding. And He commanded him to enjoy the rest, but to abstain from the tree of knowledge, and He foretold that death would be the penalty of transgression. The paradise is watered by a river, and from there this river goes forth, divided into four. The name of the one is Pishon, which means "multitude"; among the Greeks this is named the Ganges, which traverses India and empties into the sea. The second is called Gihon; the name signifies the one that empties from the east, which Josephus says the Greeks call the Nile. After this is the Tigris, which the same writer says is also called Diglath, the name conveying what is sharp together with narrowness. The remaining one is the Euphrates, that is, Phora—either "flower" or "dispersion." And both of these flow into the Red Sea. And God presented all the animals to Adam, who set a name upon each kind of them. And God created the woman, taking one of the ribs of Adam while he slept, and brought her to him. And he recognized her as having come from himself, and named her woman; for among the Hebrews woman is called "Eve," and she had been named Eve. There was, then, a blessed way of life for the two of them in paradise, since they were naked in their simplicity and lived an artless life. But they are envied by the serpent, or rather by the intelligible dragon. And the serpent approaches the woman and counsels her to taste of the plant of understanding. (Josephus says that at that time all the animals spoke the same language.) And she is persuaded, and being pleased with the eating, she persuades her husband too to share in the fruit. And they knew themselves to be naked, and out of fig leaves they made themselves girdles, and Adam and the woman hid themselves from God because of their nakedness. And God asked the reason, and Adam put forward his nakedness and fastened the blame upon the woman; and she said she had been deceived by the serpent. And God, having first cursed the serpent and deprived it of feet and taken away its voice (according to Josephus), and commanded it to crawl upon the ground, and declared it an enemy to the seed of those who had been deceived, turns to the woman, and makes her subject to her husband, and lays upon her the pangs of childbearing. Then He brings Adam too under a penalty; and this was his being turned back toward the earth from which he was taken, and the eating of his bread in sweat, and the earth's sending up thorns and thistles for him. And He removes them from paradise, clothing them in garments of skin—perhaps the coarser, mortal, and resistant flesh. From this comes our wretched and painful life, and our proneness to slip into evil.

3. Children, then, are born to them, of whom Cain was the first—the name means "possession," because they had gained possession of a man—and Abel was the second; the name signifies "mourning," for through him mourning was to come upon them. And Abel was a herdsman of a flock and gave heed to virtue, while Cain tilled the earth and was utterly wicked. When it seemed good to them to bring firstfruits from their own labors to God, Abel offered the better of the firstborn of his beasts, while Cain offered whatever came to hand of the fruits of the earth. And God gave heed to the gifts of Abel, but to the offering of Cain He did not give heed. And he, envying because of the preference, kills his brother, and becomes accursed before God, and is condemned to groan and to tremble. And being cast out from the presence of God, he dwelt in the land of Nod, where he also begot children. This man devised measures and weights and was the first to fix boundaries of land, having proved himself a guide to wickedness. And he built a city after the name of his firstborn son, Enoch. The son of Enoch was Gaidad, and his child was Maviael, whose son was Methuselah, whose son was Lamech. This man, having taken to himself two wives, who were named Adah and Zillah, had from both of them seventy-seven children; of whom Jabal was a herdsman of cattle and loved the keeping of sheep, while Jubal devised music and contrived the lyre and the psaltery, and Tubal, born of Zillah, was a smith, that is, a worker of iron and bronze.
And to Adam, after the death of Abel, when he was two hundred and thirty years old, another son was born, whom he called Seth. And Adam died, having lived nine hundred and thirty years. And Seth, when he was two hundred and five years old, begot Enos, who first hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God—that is, to address the Lord as God. And Seth, having lived in all nine hundred and twelve years, and having left sons and daughters, departed. He pursued virtue and left behind his descendants as imitators of it; and they understood the wisdom concerning the heavenly bodies, and they inscribed their discoveries upon two pillars, the one made of stones and the other of brick, so that they might be preserved for those who came after; for Adam had foretold that there would be a destruction of all things by fire and by water. And from Enos was born Kenan, and other sons and daughters, and he died, having lived nine hundred and five years. And from Kenan there sprang Mahalalel and other children, and he died, having lived a count of nine hundred and ten years. The son of Mahalalel was Jared, and others, who ended his life at eight hundred and ninety-five years. Jared was the father of Enoch and of other children after him, and he died, having lived nine hundred and sixty-two years. The son of Enoch was Methuselah, and others. And Enoch pleased the Lord and was translated and was not found, having been three hundred and sixty-five years old. The son of Methuselah was Lamech, and others, and he dies, having lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years. And Noah was born to Lamech, and Lamech died, having lived seven hundred and

4. seven and fifty-three years. And to Noah three sons were born: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
And when the sons of God saw the daughters of men, they took to themselves wives. By "sons of God" Scripture means the descendants of Seth, as pursuing virtue, just as it also calls the virtuous "sons of the Most High"; and by "daughters of men" it means those descended from the offspring of Cain. But Josephus says that angels took the daughters of men, having so named them, I suppose, as those well pleasing to God and following their manner of life. But men, being multiplied, inclined toward evil; and to them were born children, insolent and reckless through their confidence in their strength. With these the Divine was angered, and cut short their length of life, limiting the life of men to a hundred and twenty years.

But Noah found grace before God. Therefore, when the dry land was changed into sea through a rainfall of many days and great violence, all the human race perished, but Noah alone was saved by the providence of God in a wooden chest, which he had built four-square, with a length of three hundred cubits, a breadth of fifty, and a depth of thirty. Into it he himself and his sons embarked, and the mother and their wives, having placed within it seeds of every kind and animals of every kind for the preservation of their species—two of the unclean, but seven of each kind of the clean. Now Noah was the tenth counting from Adam, and after one thousand six hundred and fifty-six years the flood was brought upon the earth, for forty days a violent rain pouring down upon the earth, so that the water rose fifteen cubits above the highest of the mountains. And when the rain had ceased and the water was diminishing, after a hundred and fifty days the chest ran aground on a certain mountain of Armenia in the seventh month. At that time Noah, having opened it, sends forth a raven; and it did not return. And after some days he let go a dove, which again came back. And when seven days had passed, he let it go again, and it came back bearing a sprig of olive. And from this he knew that the water had failed from the earth. And Noah went out, and his wife and his sons with their wives, and the animals that were with them in the ark, and he sacrificed to God. Josephus says that the place in Armenia is called Apobaterion ("the place of disembarking"), and that remains of the chest are shown there. And he says that many of those who wrote the histories of the barbarian peoples make mention of the flood and of the ark—Berosus the Chaldaean, and Hieronymus the Egyptian, who wrote the antiquities of Phoenicia, and Mnaseas of Damascus. And God promised no longer to bring such a calamity upon the earth. And He commanded them to use the animals for food, save only that they should not eat flesh with the blood of the soul in it, and that they should keep from the murder of men. And as a sign that He would no longer flood the earth with rain He set the bow in the cloud, signifying the rainbow by "the bow." And Noah, having lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood, dies, having been nine hundred and fifty years old.
These things have been said by Josephus concerning the long life of those men of that time. Let no one, then, judging by present life and the brevity of years, suppose the things recorded about the ancients to be false. For being dear to God and made by God Himself, and because their nourishment was better suited for a longer span, they reasonably lived so great a number of years; and then, too, on account of the usefulness of the things they devised, astronomy and geometry, which they could not have understood and stated with certainty had they not lived six hundred years; for it is in so many years that the Great Year is fulfilled.

5. The sons of Noah—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—settled from the mountains into the plains. And Noah, having planted a vineyard, drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered. And Ham, seeing the nakedness of his father, told his brothers, as though in mockery of his father. But they, putting the garment upon their backs, covered their father's nakedness, going backwards and not looking upon their father. Therefore, when Noah had come to himself, he requited the others with blessings, but cursed Ham. And the plain in which the sons of Noah dwelt was called Shinar. And as many children were born to each and went forward into generations, their descendants were multiplied. Now a certain Nimrod, a grandson of Ham, who first appeared as a giant upon the earth, bold and mighty of hand, taking the lead over the rest, turned affairs toward tyranny, and proposed to them to build a tower, made of baked brick and bitumen. And God, seeing them thus gone mad, made them of different tongues and unable to understand one another's speech, through the division of languages. And the place in which they were building the tower is now called Babylon, because of the confusion concerning speech; for the Hebrews call confusion "Babel." And thereafter they are scattered by the diversity of tongues, so that every continent and island was filled with them.

When the descendants of Noah had been scattered, the nations were formed and named from them. Japheth, then, begot seven sons, who went forth from the mountains Taurus and Amanus—in Asia as far as the river Tanais, and in Europe as far as Gadeira; and from their names nations too were called: the Gomarites from Gomer, who are now called Galatians; Magog named those descended from him Magogites, and they are now called Scythians. From Javan the Ionians and all the Greeks were named, and from Madai the Madaeans, who are now called Medes. Tubal named those from him Thobelians; these are the Iberians. Meshech founded the race of the Meschenians; these are reckoned to be the Cappadocians. Tiras called those from him Tirasians, who were later renamed Thracians. And of the descendants of Japheth, those called Rheginians were brought forth from Ashkenaz, while the Riphathaeans—so they formerly called the Paphlagonians—are believed to draw their descent from Riphath; and the Thorgamaeans inscribe Thorgama as their ancestor, who were later renamed Phrygians. Elisha became the founder of the Elisaeans, who are the Aeolians. And Tarshish was the ancestor of the Tarshishaeans; for in old times the Cilicians were called Tarshishaeans, whence the most notable of the cities among them is called Tarsus, the theta having been changed into tau; for so it is written by Josephus concerning Tarsus. But others say that Perseus, having come to the country of the Cilicians and wishing to found a city, in showing the builders the site of the city struck the ground with the sole of his foot, and from this the city was named Tarsus. And Kittim settled the island Chettima; this is Cyprus, so called by the Greeks because of the goddess among them, Aphrodite, whom they call Cypris.
The sons of Ham held the land from Syria and the mountains Amanus and Lebanon, and they seized whatever of it faced the sea, as far as the ocean. And from Cush came the Cushites; these are the Ethiopians. Mizraim became the forefather of the Mestraeans; so the Egyptians are called, and the country of Egypt is named Mestren. Phut settled Libya, and called the people of the country Phutians, and the country itself Phute. But its name was afterward changed to Libya, from Libyos a son of Mizraim. Canaan, settling the land later called Judaea, named it Canaanitis and those from it Canaanites. The sons of Mizraim held the land from Gaza to Egypt. Only the portion of Philistim preserved its name, which the Greeks have named Palestine. Sidonios, the firstborn son of Canaan, raised up a city in Phoenicia, calling it Sidon. Amathi founded the city Amathe, which the Macedonians renamed Epiphaneia after one of the Ptolemies called Epiphanes.
To Shem the son of Noah five children are born, who dwell in Asia as far as the ocean toward India, beginning from the Euphrates. Elam, then, left the Elamites, who are the founders of the Persians; Asshur settles the city Nineveh and named those under him Assyrians; and Arphaxad was the forefather of the Chaldaeans; Aram named those later called Syrians Aramaeans after himself; and Lud brought forth the Ludians, who were afterward called Lydians. And of the sons of Aram, who were four, one settles Trachonitis and Damascus, which lies between Palestine and Coele-Syria, another settles Armenia, and the other the Bactrians. The son of Arphaxad was Kenan, and the son of Kenan was Salah. He was the father of Eber. And Eber begot Peleg, so called because of the division of the earth; for when the division of the men of that time took place, then too came the division of the earth; for the Hebrews name division "phalek." And the nation of the Hebrews was called from Eber in the beginning. The son of Peleg was Reu, and Reu was the father of Serug, who begot Nahor, and from Nahor came Terah, and from Terah Abraham.

6. The forefather of the race of the Hebrews and the patriarch of his line was this great Abraham, who was a Chaldaean by descent, the tenth from Noah, two hundred and ninety-two years having passed since God flooded the whole earth with rain. He, being of impious forebears, was the first to know one God, the Maker of all, having grasped the Maker from His works, and he said that to this God alone honor must be rendered. And when, on account of this, the Chaldaeans rose against him, he removed from there at the command of the God who had become known to him, and took possession of the land of Canaan. But when famine pressed upon Canaan, he migrates into Egypt. And being admired for his understanding, he hands down to the Egyptians, who were ignorant of these things, arithmetic and the matters concerning astronomy. And these are said to have passed from the Chaldaeans to Egypt and from there to the Greeks. When the Assyrians came against the Sodomites, among whom Lot also dwelt—being the nephew of Abraham and brother of Sarah—and many of the Sodomites had fallen and the rest had been taken captive, Lot too had been taken captive with the Sodomites. Learning this, Abraham, with three hundred and eighteen of his servants and three friends, pursued after the Assyrians, and saved both the Sodomites and Lot. And as he was returning from the pursuit, the king of the city Solyma received him, called Melchizedek—which, rendered into the language of the Greeks, means "righteous king"; for Solyma was then the name of the city Jerusalem; so ancient was the city, and by length of time it had obtained precedence over all. And God, having approved Abraham for his virtue, promised him a recompense for it; but when Abraham said that every benefaction seemed to him without grace, since he had no one to inherit it—for he was still without legitimate offspring, because Sarah's womb was barren—God promised to give him a child also, and that from him a great nation would come forth, equal in number to the stars; and He commanded that he himself and the males under him should be circumcised, so that his race might be unmixed with the other nations; and they were circumcised.
There is born, then, to Abraham, when he was a hundred years old, a child from Sarah, whom God ordered to be named Isaac; the name means "laughter," either because it was a cause of smiling to Sarah that she should bear a child, when God had so declared, on account of the unlikelihood of the promise, since she was past the prime of age and did not expect to bear—for she happened to be ninety years old when she bore Isaac—or because the child became to its parents a cause of laughter, that is, of gladness and joy. And the father circumcised this child on the eighth day after his birth; whence it is the custom among the Jews too to be circumcised in this way. But the Arabs are accustomed to circumcise their children after the thirteenth year, because Ishmael their forefather was circumcised at this age; for he was thirteen years old when God commanded the circumcision to Abraham. And this name means "God-heard," since God hearkened to the supplication of Abraham and gave him a child. And he begot him from a maidservant whom Sarah laid beside him. For being herself at that time without offspring, she asked her husband to have intercourse with her own maidservant, named Hagar, an Egyptian by race; and when she had borne Ishmael, Sarah made the child her own. But when she had borne Isaac, she condemned Hagar with her son to flight, out of jealousy. When Isaac had come to manhood—according to the Hebrew Josephus, who says that Isaac was then twenty-five years old—God brings a test upon Abraham, and calling him He commands him to offer his son as a sacrifice, and to lead his only-begotten, his beloved, to one of the mountains and offer him as a whole burnt offering. And Abraham did not refuse, but taking his child and leading him up to the mountain appointed to him, he shares with him the divine oracle, and exhorts him to bear the consecration nobly, at God's command. And he is persuaded and willingly offers himself for the consecration, saying that it was not right to resist the will of God and his father. So these things are recorded by Josephus. Then Abraham is commanded to spare his son, and a ram is given in his stead of its own accord for the whole burnt offering. After this Sarah dies, being a hundred and twenty-seven years old, and Abraham took another wife, called Keturah, from whom six sons are born to him. And to Isaac, when he was about forty years old, his father betroths Rebekah from Mesopotamia, the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother. Then Abraham dies, having lived a hundred and seventy-five years. And Isaac, having married Rebekah, begets twin children from her; of whom upon the elder thick hair grew over the whole body, whence he was called Esau, on account of the hairiness; while the younger held with his hand the heel of his brother, having sprung forth before him from the mother's womb, wherefore he was named Jacob; and the name means "supplanter" among the Hebrews.

7. After these things Isaac grows old and is blinded in his eyes. And he summons Esau—for he was attached to him because of the rights of the firstborn—and bids him to hunt and to prepare a meal for him, "so that," he says, "having eaten, I may bless you before I die." And Esau went out to the hunt; but Rebekah, loving Jacob more, called him too and told him what his father had commanded Esau, and urged him to hasten to the flock and bring her two tender kids, that from these she might prepare for the old man the kind of dish she knew he loved, and that having eaten he might bless him. And he does according to his mother's commands. And when the dishes were already prepared, she wraps the arms of the boy with the skins of the kids, and gives him the meal to take to his father. But Isaac, perceiving by the voice that the one approaching was Jacob, summons him very near and feels his hands. And since God had in any case judged Esau unworthy of the blessing, it seemed to Isaac that his firstborn stood before him—he was perhaps deceived by the thickness of the hair—and having eaten he blessed Jacob. And Esau too returned and brought a meal to his father and asked for the blessing. But he understood the trick and said, "Your brother came and took your blessing." And when he lamented and demanded to be blessed—since there was not, he said, a single blessing left with him—Isaac, moved to compassion, set out to bless him; but because it did not seem to the divine Spirit that prompted him that Esau should obtain a blessing, since he was not worthy of it, the words of Isaac were shaped for him into a curse instead of a blessing. On account of these things Esau was hostile toward his brother. And Jacob, fearing his brother, departs into Mesopotamia by his mother's counsel. And as he was going, he is deemed worthy in his sleep of the famous vision of the ladder, of which the one end was set upon the earth and the other upon heaven, and he is initiated into things to come by the Higher Power, and the place in which he saw the vision he called Bethel; which means "divine hearth" among the Greeks. And having come to Haran, he was brought to Laban, the brother of his mother Rebekah, and obtained hospitality from him and is entrusted with the care of the flocks. Now Laban had two daughters, of whom the elder was called Leah and the other Rachel; and Jacob was stirred to love of the younger, who was comely in form beyond her sister, and he brings words to Laban concerning her. And he agrees to give Rachel in marriage to Jacob, if he will serve him for seven years. The lover consents to this; the time passes; the father-in-law prepares the marriage; but by night he lays the elder of his daughters beside Jacob. And learning by day that he had been deceived, he charges his father-in-law with wrongdoing. But he promised Rachel to him as well, after the service of another seven years. Jacob is persuaded again to serve, being enslaved by love, and after another seven years he is also wedded to Rachel.
Now to Leah there were children by Jacob. And she calls the firstborn Reuben, because he came to her by the mercy of God; for she was grieved that her sister was beloved by her husband, and she expected rather to become more honored if she should conceive in her womb. And the second she names Simeon; this means that God became a hearer to her. And after him Levi is born; the name means "confirmer." After whom Judah is born to her; the name signifies "thanksgiving." But Rachel had no child, and fearing that on account of her childlessness she should be esteemed less, she asks her husband to go in to her maidservant. And he is persuaded and goes in to Bilhah, and Bilhah bears a child from Jacob, and the child was called Dan; the Greeks would say "God-judged." And from the same maid again is born Naphtali, "resourceful," as it were, because she contrived in rivalry against her sister's good fortune in children. At these things Leah is jealous, and she too lays her own maidservant Zilpah beside Jacob. And she too bore a son, Gad; one might call him "the chance-born." And after him she bears another, who was Asher; he might be called "the blessing-bringer," as having become a cause of good repute and felicitation to Leah on account of her many children. And when Reuben, the son of Leah, had brought mandrake apples, Rachel asked her to share some of them with her, and offered her sister in exchange the bed of Jacob on that night; for that night had been allotted to Rachel. And on account of this Jacob is wedded to Leah, and the woman bears yet two more children, Issachar—the name signifies "the one born from hire"—and Zebulun, which means "the one pledged by goodwill toward her"—and a daughter called Dinah. And to Rachel too a son, Joseph, is born; the name signifies the addition of someone to come.

8. Now for twenty years Jacob shepherded for his father-in-law; then, wishing to withdraw, he was not permitted. Therefore he fled secretly with his wives, together with the maidservants and the children, taking along his possessions and the flocks that had been allotted to him as wages for shepherding. And Rachel also carried off the idols of her father—not as honoring them, but that she might have these as a refuge, if her father, pursuing them, should overtake them. And when Laban overtook them on the seventh day, God commanded him in a dream to make a treaty with Jacob. By day there are words between the two, and when Jacob had shown that he did no wrong, Laban charged him concerning the ancestral gods. But he, conscious of nothing concerning them, allowed him to search. And he searched. But Rachel had placed the idols in the saddle of the camel that bore her, and she sat upon it, saying that the flow of her monthly periods was troubling her. And Laban, thinking that his daughter would never approach his gods with such an affliction, passed her by. And he turned back; but Jacob, fearing his brother, sends ahead a message declaring to him his return, and dispatches gifts to him. And when night came on, meeting with a phantom he wrestled with it and seemed to prevail. And perceiving that it was an angel of God, he begged it to tell him what fortune he would have; and it said that the prevailing over a divine angel must be deemed a sign of great good things, and bade him be called Israel. This name some interpret as "a mind seeing God," but Josephus says it signifies "one who withstood a divine angel." And Jacob calls the place Peniel, that is, "the face of God." And since a pain arose in him during the wrestling with the angel, about the broad sinew, he renounced the eating of it, and on his account it is forbidden also to all his race. When Esau met his brother, they came together and embraced. Then Esau departed, and Jacob came to Shechem. And while the Shechemites were keeping a festival, his daughter Dinah went into the city to see the festival. So Shechem, the son of the king of the city, beholding her, defiled her by violence. Then his father begged Jacob to give Dinah in marriage to Shechem; but he would not consent. And Simeon and Levi, the brothers of the girl by the same mother, while those in the city were feasting on account of the festival and were heavy-headed, going in by night, slew every male of full age, and the king and his son. So Josephus says. But the book of Genesis records these things more credibly. For it says that, when Hamor the father of Shechem asked that Dinah be married to his son, Simeon and Levi said, "If all the males in the city should be circumcised, we will give our sister to your son," and that they accepted the proposal and were all circumcised. And on the third day after the circumcision, while those who had been circumcised were in a bad state and in pain from the inflammation, they fell upon them and slew them all, without Jacob's knowledge. And when he was angry at these things, God bade him take courage. And Jacob, having come to Bethel, where he had seen the dream, sacrificed. And going on, he buries Rachel, who had died in childbirth, at Ephratha. And the child born from her he called Benjamin, on account of the pain that befell its mother at his birth. And coming to Hebron, a city of the Canaanites, he found his father Isaac still living, but Rebekah had died beforehand. And after a little while Isaac too dies, and is buried with his wife in the ancestral tomb, having lived a hundred and eighty-five years.
Now Esau ruled over Idumaea, having called the country after himself. For he was called Edom, because, returning once from the hunt famished, and finding his brother having prepared lentils for himself as food, he asked him to give him some; but Jacob compelled him to sell him his birthright in exchange for the lentils. And Esau yields it to him with oaths on account of the famine; whence he was called Edom, on account of the yellowness of the lentils; for they were exceedingly of such a color. And among the Hebrews "Edom" means "red."

9. Now Jacob loved Joseph, the son of Rachel, more than the other children, both for the goodliness of his body and for the virtue of his soul. And indeed his father's affection, and the dreams that he saw, stirred his brothers to envy of him. Of the dreams the one was of this kind: in the season of summer he seemed, while reaping with his brothers, to be binding sheaves and setting them up, and his own remained at rest, while those of his brothers ran up and did obeisance to his. The other was this: the sun and the moon and the rest of the stars seemed to him to do obeisance to him. When he had related these visions to his father, in the presence of his brothers, he asked to learn their meaning. And he proclaimed good fortune to the child, and that a time would come in which he would be honored and venerated by his parents and his brothers. These things grieved the brothers of Joseph, and they looked askance at the youth. And while the sons of Jacob were grazing the flocks at Shechem, the father sends Joseph to look after them. But they, seeing him, set out to kill him. Reuben, however, counseled them not to become the slayers of their brother with their own hands, but to throw him into a pit nearby, that he might die there, and so the evil would be more moderate. And when the young men assented to the proposal, Reuben, taking the youth, gently let him down into the pit. But Judah, seeing Arab merchants, counseled his brothers to sell Joseph to them. And when this seemed good to them, they sell him to the merchants for twenty minae, being seventeen years old. And Reuben, coming to the pit by night, that he might bring up Joseph and save him without his brothers' knowledge, when he did not find him, in his grief reproached his brothers. But when they told what had been done, he ceases from his grief. And having stained the boy's tunic with the blood of a he-goat, they came to their father and said that they had neither seen Joseph nor known how he had perished, but had found this tunic bloodied and torn. And Jacob sat mourning for the youth, having put on sackcloth. Now Joseph was bought from the merchants by Potiphar, an Egyptian, the chief of the cooks of King Pharaoh, and he held him in honor. But when the wife of his master, on account of his comeliness and his adroitness, was disposed amorously toward him and brought words concerning intercourse, he put aside her demand. And she, sorely besieged by love, brought a second attempt, and despairing of persuasion she wished to use force. And when the young man, leaving his garment behind, leapt out, she sat downcast and confounded. And when her husband came, she accused Joseph and displayed the garment, as though he had left it when he was attempting to use force. And Potiphar casts Joseph into the prison of evildoers, in which the cupbearer of Pharaoh too was shut up in anger, and the chief baker. Having become familiar with these men, he was asked to tell them the meaning of their dreams. For the cupbearer thought he saw a vine, from which three branches grew, on which hung great and ripe clusters, and that he pressed these into a cup and brought it to Pharaoh, and that he received it. Joseph interpreted that the dream signified good things for him; for within the three days following he would be restored to his former office. And he asked that, when he had prospered, he would remember him. But the chief baker said that he seemed to be carrying three baskets upon his head, two full of bread, the other of cooked food and various viands, and that these were snatched away by birds flying down upon them. And Joseph said to this man too that the three baskets signified three days, and that on the third day he was to be hanged and become food for flesh-eating birds. And it came to pass for both of them as Joseph had interpreted.

10. Then God sends upon Pharaoh two visions of dreams, and the meanings of both. But he remembered the visions and forgot the interpretations. So he summons together the wise men of the Egyptians and reports to them the dreams and demands the meaning; and when they were at a loss, he was angry. And the cupbearer, if not before, yet then came to remember Joseph, and tells Pharaoh about him. So he is led in at once. And Pharaoh says, "Tell me, young man, the interpretation of the dreams that I have seen. I thought that seven well-fed oxen, coming up out of the river, went toward the marsh; and that seven others, lean and wasted with hunger, coming out of the marsh, met these, and that the first and fat ones were devoured by the second, and that they remained still lean as before. And again I see seven ears of grain growing from a single root, flourishing and bowed by the weight of the fruit. And near them I seemed to see an equal number of ears, feeble from lack of dew and unpleasant to the sight, which consumed those that were fruitful and fair." And Joseph says, "Although the dreams are twofold, O king, they have one meaning of things to come. For the oxen, an animal that labors at the plow, devoured by the worse; and the flourishing ears wasted away by the feeble—these announce a famine for so many years upon your country, in an equal number of years previously flourishing in fruits, so that the abundance of these will be consumed by what comes after. But if you store up the goods of the former prosperity for the years of barrenness, you will make the misfortune imperceptible to the Egyptians." And Pharaoh, struck with amazement at Joseph's wisdom on account of the interpretation and the counsel, said, "You yourself shall be the judge and counselor and steward of the things resolved upon." And he gave him his authority, so that he used Pharaoh's seal and clothed himself in purple and rode upon a chariot. Joseph was then thirty years old. And Pharaoh named him Psothomphanech; the name means "discoverer of hidden things." And he joined to him also a wife, called Asenath, the daughter of the chief of the priests in Heliopolis. From her children are born to him before the famine, of whom the elder was Manasseh—the name means "forgetting," because he found forgetfulness of his misfortunes—and the younger was Ephraim, which means "rendering back," because the freedom of his forefathers was rendered back to him. From there came the time of want. And the famine prevailed not only over Egypt, but also over the country in which Jacob dwelt. So he sends his sons into Egypt to buy grain, keeping only Benjamin with himself as the youngest. They, then, came to Joseph. And he, not recognized, recognized his brothers, and said that they had come as spies. But they told from where they came, and that they were of one father, still living, and that there was another younger brother with the father. And Joseph said that they would give him assurance of the truth, if they would bring the younger brother to him. So he gives them grain, and secretly placing the silver in the sack of each; but he kept Simeon to be a hostage for their return. The sons came back to Jacob bringing the grain, and reported what had happened, and the holding back of Simeon caused him grief, and he would not consent to let Benjamin be taken to Egypt. But when the grain had already been spent, since it was not otherwise possible for them to go to Egypt unless they brought Benjamin too, the father, yielding to necessity, gives him, and double the price of the grain, and gifts for Joseph. And when they came to Egypt, they brought him the gifts. But he, seeing Benjamin and being deeply moved, withdrew, that he might not become visible in his tears. Then he takes the brothers to a meal, and honored Benjamin with double portions, and bids the steward of the grain to give them grain and to put the price into the sacks, and into Benjamin's load to throw also a silver cup. When these things had been done, the brothers departed, taking Simeon. But horsemen surround them as they were leaving, charging them with the theft of the cup, and searching they found the cup by Benjamin's load. So the horsemen led Benjamin to Joseph, and his brothers, rending their robes, wept and followed along. And Joseph, having reproached them as ungrateful, set the rest free, but was content with the holding of Benjamin alone. And helplessness gripped them. But Judah, speaking and pleading much that was moving toward compassion, brought Joseph to a breaking of his feeling. And he, no longer able to feign anger, makes himself known to his brothers, and acknowledged his thanks to them as fellow-causes of what had been resolved by God concerning him. "Go, then," he says, "and declare these things to my father, and taking him and all the kindred, remove here; for there will be famine for five years more." Saying this, he embraces his brothers and honors them with gifts.

11. And they departed; and Jacob, learning about Joseph, set out at once to him, taking along all who were with him; and they were seventy-five. And when he was already near Egypt, Joseph meets him. And from joy he all but fainted. And when Pharaoh heard that Jacob and those with him had come to Egypt, he was glad, and when Jacob came to him he greeted him. And learning that those with him were shepherds, he granted them dwelling in Heliopolis. And as the famine grew worse, Joseph gave out the grain to the Egyptians for money. And when this failed, they bought it with their cattle, then they yielded up even their land, that they might be fed. And so, when Pharaoh had become master of all property except that of the priests—for to these their land remained—when the famine had now abated, Joseph, gathering the Egyptians each to his own city, gave them back the land and exhorted them to industry, paying the fifth of the fruits to Pharaoh. And Jacob, having passed seventeen years in Egypt, fell sick and departed, foretelling how those of his line were to dwell in Canaan. And to the rest of his sons he prayed for the gaining of good things; but of Joseph he recounted a eulogy, that he had not borne a grudge against his brothers, and he commanded his sons that they should reckon the children of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, as their own, dividing Canaan together with these. And when Joseph had presented his sons to Jacob to be blessed, he set the elder by the right hand, and the younger by the left. But he, placing his hands crosswise upon the heads of the children, assigned the right hand to the younger, and to the elder the left. And when Joseph said to his father that the laying on of hands ought not to be done thus, he was not persuaded to alter the arrangement of his hands. For it was not, as Joseph supposed, that he did not know what he was doing, harmed in his understanding by the depth of his old age; rather, as a prophet he was hinting at things to come, and prefigured the saving cross, and showed that the new people, that is, the people from the nations, would be reckoned at the right hand by God and preferred to the elder—I mean, that is, the Jewish people. And Jacob dies, having lived a hundred and forty-seven years. And Joseph, with Pharaoh's consent, goes to Hebron and buries his father lavishly. And when his brothers feared to return with him, lest, remembering the wrong, he should requite them, he persuaded them to suspect nothing. And he too dies, having lived a hundred and ten years, having commanded that, when those of his line should migrate from Egypt, they should carry up his bones also and bring them into Canaan.

12. But the Egyptians, seeing the Israelites flourishing and having forgotten Joseph, devised various afflictions against them. For they ordered them to cut the river into very many channels, and to build walls for the cities and to raise up embankments, that by these the river might be kept from forming a lake, and to set up pyramids; and with these labors they wore down the Hebrews. For a long time, then, they passed in these very hardships. Then one of the sacred scribes announces to Pharaoh that there would be born at that time among the Israelites one who, when grown, would humble the Egyptians but exalt his own kindred. So Pharaoh, taking fright, commands that every male born to the Hebrews be destroyed by being cast into the river, and that the parents of children who did not do this be killed with their whole household, and that the Egyptian midwives watch over the childbirths of the Hebrew women.
And while they were in these straits, a certain man of noble birth was grievously distressed at these things, for his wife was with child, and he prayed to God. And God commanded him in his sleep not to despair. "For the child," He said, "whom the Egyptians suspect will be yours, and will be saved and reared, escaping the notice of those who plot, and will release his kinsmen from the slavery among the Egyptians, and will obtain everlasting remembrance. And his brother will serve me as priest, with his descendants, forever." So his wife bears him a male child, escaping the notice of the guards, and the babe is reared by its parents for three months. But fearing, they entrusted his safety to God, and contriving a kind of basket and smearing it round with bitumen, they put the babe in it and let it go down the river. And the child's sister, Mariamme, watched what would happen. Now while she was playing by the banks of the river, Thermouthis, the daughter of Pharaoh, sees the basket, and sending, she fetches it. And seeing the child, she loved it, both for its beauty and for its size. And Egyptian women are brought to suckle it; but it would not take their breast. And Mariamme, as if happening to be present, said, "O queen, if a Hebrew woman should be called, perhaps the babe will accept the breast of one of its own kind." And she said, "Call her." And she brought the mother, and Thermouthis entrusted the child's nursing to her for wages, and from what had happened she names it. For the Egyptians call water "mo," and those saved from water "yses"; so, putting together both words, she used them as the name of the babe. Now Moses was the seventh from Abraham; for he himself was the son of Amram, and Kohath was the father of Amram, and he was the son of Levi, and Levi was the son of Jacob, and Jacob was born to Isaac, and Isaac sprang from Abraham. When the child was three years old, both the height of his stature and the grace of his form became distinguished by a more divine charm, and his understanding grew far greater than his age. So Thermouthis, being without offspring of her own, adopts him and brings him to her father; and he, embracing the child to his breast, places upon him in affection the diadem. And the child, as if in childish play, throws it to the ground and trampled it with his feet. When the sacred scribe—who had foretold that one of the Hebrews would arise to humble the rule of the Egyptians—saw this, he cried out and said, "This is that child, by whose destruction you may take away the fear of the Egyptians." But Thermouthis forestalled him by snatching the child away, and God made Pharaoh sluggish toward the murder.
And when Moses, after such a beginning, came to manhood, he became manifest to the Egyptians for his virtue. The Ethiopians, neighbors of Egypt, were ravaging their country, and the Egyptians make war upon them; and they were defeated, and the Ethiopians, despising them, wore down the whole of Egypt. And by a divine oracle Pharaoh asks his daughter for Moses, now come to manhood, that he might be their general against the Ethiopians. And she gives him, having put her father under oath to do him no harm. And Moses, entrusted with the war, leads the army against the enemy not by the customary road, but by an untrodden one, full of venomous reptiles; and there too he displayed his understanding. For having made baskets and filled them with ibises—which Egypt rears many and tame—he carried these along that road; and the ibises are enemies to these venomous creatures; and using them as champions, going before the army, against the venomous creatures, he came upon the Ethiopians, who had no forewarning, and conquers them and takes not a few of their cities. And they, driven together into Saba, a city that was the royal seat of Ethiopia—which Cambyses later named Meroe after his sister of the same name—were besieged; but the city was hard to besiege. And Tharbis, the daughter of the ruler of the Ethiopians, slipped into love of Moses and sends to him concerning marriage; and he consented, if she should hand over the city to him. The deed forestalled the words, and Moses celebrated the marriage, and led the Egyptians back to their own land. But they hated him even while they were being saved by him, and incited Pharaoh against him. And he, both persuaded by the sacred scribes and on account of the killing of the Egyptian who was scourging the Hebrew—as is contained in the book of Genesis, even if Josephus passed this over—set himself to the slaying of Moses. But Moses, though the roads were guarded, slipped away unnoticed through the wilderness, and goes to the city of Midian, and is received as a guest by the priest of the city, who, bearing two names, was called both Reuel and Jethro. And he gives his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage, and makes him a shepherd of his flocks.

13. Now while Moses was pasturing his flock toward Mount Sinai, he is deemed worthy of the vision of the bush, which fire burned but did not consume. Then he hears a voice from there, which commanded him not to come forward, since the place was holy, and foretold things to come, and ordered him to go to Egypt to free his kinsmen from their affliction there and to lead them out of Egypt, and commanded him to offer sacrifices in that place. These things Moses heard from God out of the fire. But he was at a loss how he should either persuade his own people or constrain Pharaoh to permit the departure. And God promised that He would accomplish these things most easily for him, and, as proof, Moses is commanded to throw his staff to the ground, and when he had thrown it, it became a serpent, then when he took hold of it again, it was a staff. And being commanded to put his right hand into his bosom, he drew it out white as chalk in color, then it was restored to its former appearance. And being bidden to take some of the water nearby and pour it on the ground, he sees what was poured out turned to blood. He was therefore exhorted to take courage at these signs and no longer to delay. Taking, then, his wife and the sons from her—Gershom, which means "into a foreign land," and Eleazar, which signifies that he had used the ancestral God as ally—he set out for Egypt. And as he drew near, his brother Aaron met him. So both come to Pharaoh, and stating the commands from God, they asked him not to act against the divine will. And when he scoffed, they showed the signs in deed, and the rod, when thrown, became a serpent. And when the Egyptian sorcerers had done the same and changed their own staffs into serpents, Moses throws his staff again to the ground, and being changed into a serpent, it devoured the staffs of the Egyptians, which appeared as serpents; then he takes it up again when it had fallen back into its own shape. And as Pharaoh hardened himself, the waters were changed into blood. Then frogs covered the whole land of Egypt. After these, gnats sprang up from the ground. Now the other portents the sorcerers of Pharaoh seemed to produce, but they were not able to conjure up gnats. So they said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God"; but he was still unyielding. And there came the dog-fly, and after it the destruction of the cattle. Then, when Moses scattered furnace-soot into the air, sores and blisters broke out both on the cattle and on the men; and again hail rained down, and after it came the locust, and after these darkness covered the Egyptians for three days, and last of all there was brought upon them the destruction of the firstborn. For as Pharaoh hardened himself, God commanded Moses to prepare a sacrifice for the fourteenth of the month—which among the Hebrews is called Nisan, among the Egyptians Pharmuthi, among the Macedonians Xanthikos, and among the Greeks April. And when the fourteenth came, all sacrificed and anointed the doorposts of their houses with the blood of the victim, and having dined, they burned what was left of the flesh. Whence from that time the Hebrews keep a festival at this season and sacrifice, calling the festival Pascha. And some say that "Pascha" means "passage," but Josephus says it means "passing over," because on that night God, passing over the Hebrews, sent upon the Egyptians the destruction of the firstborn. Whence the Egyptians, coming together, begged Pharaoh to release the Hebrews; and he ordered them to depart. And they went out. And the number of those migrating, of military age alone, was six hundred thousand. They went out on the fifteenth of the month Xanthikos by the moon, four hundred and thirty years after Abraham's coming into Canaan, and two hundred and fifteen years after Jacob's sojourn into Egypt. Moses was then in the eightieth year of his life, and Aaron exceeded him by three. And they carried along also the bones of Joseph, fulfilling the command of the man.

14. So they departed; but the Egyptians repented, and taking up arms they pursued. They had six hundred chariots and fifty thousand horsemen and two hundred thousand foot soldiers. The Hebrews were brought to despair, since their situation had become straitened, and they were about to stone Moses. But he exhorted them to follow him, and led them to the sea, and standing beside it and calling upon God, he strikes the sea with his staff; and it was driven back and left the ground bare for the Hebrews, and they crossed in haste. Seeing this, the Egyptians too, putting their cavalry in front, pursued. But when the Hebrews had already been brought safely to the land on the opposite side, the sea was poured over the Egyptians, when Moses with his rod struck the water again in the contrary direction and united its divided parts. So all the Egyptians in the waters perished. And the Hebrews were singing hymns and rejoicing, and Moses composed a song to God, set in a hexameter measure, as Josephus says. And the arms of the Egyptians, together with their bodies cast up out of the sea by the wind, the Hebrews took and armed themselves with them. And Moses led them to Mount Sinai, to sacrifice there the thank-offerings for their deliverance, as had been commanded him. But as they were being led there, the scarcity of provisions and the lack of water grieved them. And in this state they come to a place in which there was a well, whose water was undrinkable on account of its bitterness. And the name of the place the book of Exodus calls Marah, but Josephus records that it was called Mar by the Hebrews, saying that the Hebrews call the bitter "mar." And they murmured against their leader; but he, having first prayed to God, took a piece of wood and threw it into the well and sweetened the water. Josephus, however, seems not to believe that the sweetening of the water was a miracle, but, supposing it to have been sweetened naturally, says that Moses, having thrown the wood into the water, ordered them to draw the well dry, and they labored, and the water, exercised and cleansed by the continual drawings, was now drinkable. And he healed the lack of provisions, having prayed to God, by means of quails. For a multitude of quails flew down upon the camp of the Hebrews, which they caught and ate. And after these things God rained the manna upon them, in sweetness like honey, but in size like coriander seed, and called "manna" by them, as they were at a loss what this might be; for "man" also means a question in their language. So Josephus relates these things too. And he had commanded each to gather an assaron of it each day—the assaron is a measure—but if anyone gathered more, it was uneatable on the morrow, corrupted by worms and bitterness. And this was arranged so that, the strong gathering much, there might not be a shortage for the weak. And of this food they made use for forty years, as long as they were in the wilderness. Again, then, they came to a waterless place called Rephidim, and being thirsty they were stirred against Moses. But he, having prayed to God, is commanded to strike the rock with his rod, and he strikes it, from which at once gushed forth water, abundant and very clear. But the Amalekites advanced against the Hebrews, having summoned the neighboring peoples as allies. And Moses, having separated the warlike portion of the people from the rest, and set over them Joshua the son of Nun, and left a part of the army for the guarding of the water, himself withdrew to the mountain, and commanded Joshua to trust in God and to lead the army out against the enemy. So now the battle was joined; and as long as Moses held his hands aloft, the Hebrews handled the Amalekites badly, but whenever Moses let down his hands, wearied by their lifting up, then it came to pass that the Hebrews were worsted. So setting on either side his brother Aaron and Hur, the husband of his sister Miriam, he commanded them to hold up his hands. And thus the Hebrews, conquering the Amalekites, would have destroyed them all, had not night stopped them. And of the Hebrews not one died.

15. From there they went forward, and in the third month after the departure from Egypt they came to Mount Sinai, and Moses sacrificed there to God. There too Reuel his father-in-law met him; and seeing his son-in-law beset by a press of business, with all coming to him, he counseled him to entrust the examination of lawsuits to others, but himself to take thought for the greater affairs and for the safety of the people, and to appoint rulers over thousands by ten-thousands, then over thousands, and to set others over five hundreds, and besides these to make commanders of hundreds and of fifties, and to set those who should keep order over thirties and twenties and tens. When Reuel had given this counsel, Moses does according to his suggestion. Then, having commanded the people to encamp near Mount Sinai, he himself went up the mountain; and the people encamped, keeping themselves pure both in other purity and from intercourse with women for three days. And on the third day at dawn a cloud encircled the camp of the Hebrews, and there were fearful lightnings and a violence of winds, which struck the Hebrews with terror as they waited at their tents. But Moses appears, full of courage, and being seen he frees them from their fear and declares to them what God had commanded and what laws they should keep, and he brings the people, together with their wives and children, that they might hear God. And they heard a voice coming from on high. Then again he goes up to the mountain; and when he tarried there, the people gathered to Aaron, saying, "Make us gods; for as for this Moses, we do not know what has become of him." And Aaron, being pressed, ordered each to bring the golden earrings and the ornaments that their wives and daughters wore. And they brought them, and from these they made a molten calf and sacrificed to it. But Moses, coming down from the mountain and carrying in his hands the two tablets of the testimony, of stone, inscribed on both sides, when he drew near the camp, sees the calf, and in anger he shattered the tablets, and taking the calf he burned it and ground it fine and, throwing it into water, made the people drink. And he commanded the sons of Levi, and they went through the camp and killed many, so that those who fell were numbered up to three thousand. And Moses returned to the mountain, saying, "Lord, your people has sinned, and now, if you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me too out of your book." And the Lord said to him, "Go down, lead this people to the place of which I told you." And the Lord revealed to Moses, who had asked to see Him, His back parts. And he came down to the people again, carrying two tablets that had the ten words written on them, and the appearance of his face was glorified, and the people could not look steadily at him, and he put a veil about his face, and so he spoke with them. And he reported to them what God had commanded concerning sacrifices and purifications, and concerning unclean and clean animals, so that they should abstain from the one and be nourished by the other, and concerning unlawful unions, and whom the priests should take in marriage, and what kind the high priests, and concerning the Sabbath and the seventh year and the fiftieth, which they call the Jubilee; and that God had commanded a tabernacle to be made, into which He would come, brought along with them as they moved; and He showed him the measures of the tabernacle and the form according to which it should be constructed. And the people, rejoicing at these things, brought gold and silver and precious stones and bronze and wood and goat's hair and rams' skins and linen and wool. And he set as master-builders of the tabernacle the son of his sister Miriam, Bezalel, and Eliphaz.

16. When the tabernacle had now been made, Moses set it up. And the ark had been made of incorruptible wood, which gold covered on every side, in which they placed the two tablets that had the ten words inscribed on them. Of these the first says that there is one God and that He alone must be worshiped; the second, that one should make no image of any living thing nor worship it; the third, not to swear by God for any vain thing; the fourth, to observe the seventh days, resting from every work; the fifth, to honor parents; the sixth, to abstain from murder; the seventh, not to commit adultery; the eighth, not to steal; the ninth, not to bear false witness; the tenth, not to covet anything belonging to another. This ark, then, they bring into the innermost sanctuary. And in the holy place they set a table, and upon it twelve unleavened loaves, and a golden lampstand, and a censer of wood within, but covered with gold without. And before the tabernacle he set up an altar of wood, plated round with bronze scales, opposite which were placed bowls and mixing-vessels with incense-pans, and other utensils that had been prepared for the sacred service, all of gold. And robes are made for the priests, and indeed for the high priest as well. And God appointed Aaron as high priest. And Moses, gathering the multitude together, said, "Men, the work is finished, but God deems Aaron worthy of the honor of the priesthood." And Moses commanded each to bring in half a shekel, that there might be a fund for the needs concerning the tabernacle. The shekel is a Hebrew coin equal to four Attic drachmas. And the number of those contributing was six hundred and five thousand five hundred and fifty. And the contribution was made by those of the free men who had passed their twentieth year and were under the fiftieth. And the tabernacle was made in seven months. And God showed that the work had been done according to His purpose, being present in the tabernacle. And He revealed His presence thus. A mist came over the tabernacle alone, neither deep and dense and like the clouds, nor very thin and rare, so that sight could pass through it; and a pleasant dew flowed from it. And Moses sacrificed in the open court of the tabernacle for seven days, and on the eighth he proclaimed a festival to the people and commanded them to sacrifice. And they vied with one another. And when the sacred offerings were laid upon the altar, a fire was kindled of its own accord and consumed all that was upon the altar. But the elder of the four sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, having sacrificed contrary to what was ordained, were burned in the chest and the face, a fire being kindled of its own accord and consuming them; whose bodies, carried outside the camp, were buried. And he separated the tribe of Levi from the rest and consecrated it, and handed over to them the tabernacle and the sacred utensils, that, as the priests directed, they themselves might minister. After these things he resolved to number the people, and there were found, of those able to bear arms, six hundred and three thousand six hundred and fifty. These were those who had passed their twentieth year and reached the fiftieth. And in place of the tribe of Levi they reckoned among the chiefs of tribes the sons of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, according to the ordinance of their forefather Jacob. But the Levites, when numbered, were found to be twenty-three thousand eight hundred and eighty.

17. Then the multitude rose in revolt, blaming Moses because, having taken them away from a good land, he had made them wander in the wilderness. Leading them from there to the place called the Ravine, near the land of the Canaanites, he took one from each tribe and sent them to spy out both the strength of the Canaanites and the quality of the land. They, having traversed the land in forty days, returned, bringing fruits from that land, and praised the country as good, but frightened the multitude, saying that the taking of it was beyond their power, on account of the size of the rivers and the difficulty of the mountains and the strength of the cities. And the multitude again were angry with Moses, and thought to stone both him and Aaron and to return to Egypt. Only of the spies, Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb encouraged the people, asserting that nothing difficult would meet them. But Moses and Aaron supplicated God that He would stop the multitude from its folly. And the cloud was present in the tabernacle and signified the appearing of God. And Moses, taking courage, spoke to the multitude, and said that God was angry, but that He would not destroy them all nor blot out the race, yet would not give them Canaan, but would leave them in the wilderness for forty years, while to their children He would give the land. When Moses had said these things, the multitude was grieved. Then they wished to engage the Canaanites, though God forbade it; and attacking, they were defeated, and some fell, while others fled together into the camp.
Then a sedition seized the multitude from such a cause as this. Korah, being of the tribe of Levi, and most conspicuous in lineage and wealth and most persuasive in speech, had envy toward Moses and cried out against the man as exercising a tyranny. "For on what ground," he said, "did he assign the priesthood to Aaron and his sons? If because he is of the tribe of Levi, I have a juster claim to obtain it, being of like lineage but superior in wealth and age. But if it ought to be assigned to another tribe, that of Reuben will be preferred by reason of seniority, and Dathan and Abiram will receive it." These things he said with malice, and there were arrayed with him two hundred and fifty of the leading men, and the multitude too had been stirred up. But Moses, standing in the midst, said, "To me, O Korah, both you and each of those arrayed with you seem worthy of honor; but God assigned the priesthood to Aaron, and now He Himself will again judge whom He wishes to be priest. At dawn, then, all of you who lay claim to the priesthood, come forward, each bringing a censer from his house, and fire and incense; and with you likewise let Aaron come forward. And when you offer incense before the people, whosesoever sacrifice God judges the more pleasing, he shall be your priest." The multitude approved this, and on the next day they came together to the assembly. And Moses, sending to Dathan and Abiram, commanded them to come; but they, not persuaded, threatened against Moses. And Moses, bidding the chief men follow him, went to their tents, and coming near, he raised his hands to heaven and cried with a loud voice, "Since I am suspected of acting wickedly, Master, come yourself as judge, and show that nothing happens of its own accord, but all is governed by your providence. And if it was at your command that I gave the priesthood to Aaron, may the earth gape open about Dathan and Abiram and their families, on the ground on which they stand; but if they speak the truth against me, may I fall into the very things I have called down upon them." This he said weeping. And the earth is shaken all at once, and, a harsh sound being broken forth, it sank in about their tents and carried them and their belongings down into the chasm, and so what had been divided came together again. At these things the people shuddered, and Moses calls those who were contending for the priesthood. And when two hundred and fifty men of the notable ones, and Aaron and Korah, had come together before the tabernacle and consecrated upon the censers what they brought, a great fire blazed forth, such as would be kindled at God's command, by which the two hundred and fifty and Korah were destroyed, so that not even their bodies were found; only Aaron was found unharmed. And Moses ordered the censers of those men to be set about the bronze altar, that they might be a reminder of what had happened to those who came after. And convening the assembly again, he told the chiefs of the tribes to come, bringing the names of the tribes inscribed upon staffs, the priesthood being for him on whose staff a sign should come from God. So the others bring them, and Aaron, having inscribed "Levite" upon his staff. And Moses set them down in the tabernacle of God. On the next day he brought them out. And the others remained just as they were, but the staff of Aaron had sprouted branches and fruit. And the fruit the book of Leviticus calls nuts, but Josephus almonds. So all were amazed, since God had three times appointed Aaron. And since the tribe of Levi was released from wars and military service, that they might not, through lack of necessities, neglect the service of the sanctuary, Moses commanded that when the Hebrews had acquired Canaan they should apportion to the Levites forty-eight cities and land about them, and pay them the tithe of the yearly fruits, both to them and to the priests; and he ordained that the people should furnish them with very many other things, the particulars of which he who inquires will find by opening the book of Leviticus.

18. Having ordained these things, Moses came to Idumaea with the army and asked to pass through it. But the king of the country came out to meet Moses with an armed force. And he proceeded through the wilderness, since God counseled him not to begin a battle. At that time too Mariamme, the sister of Moses, died, in the fortieth year after the departure from Egypt. And he led the people through the wilderness and through Arabia; there too Aaron died, having gone up to a high mountain and handed over the high-priestly robe to his son Eleazar, in the sight of the multitude, having lived a hundred and twenty-three years. And Moses, coming to the country of the Moabites and Amorites, asked passage for the army. But Sihon, the king of the country, prevented the Hebrews from crossing, and when God signified victory to Moses, who inquired, the Hebrews, taking up their full armor, advanced to battle. The Amorites are at once routed and all destroyed, and Sihon their king fell. And they took the cities and seized their land. And Og, the king of Galadene and Gaulanitis, attacks the Israelites, having come as ally to Sihon, who had already perished. So he himself dies in the battle and his army is destroyed, and the cities were taken and the inhabitants perished. From there Moses leads the force along the great plain and encamps opposite Jericho. This is a prosperous city, bearing palms and rich in balsam. And Balak, the king of the Moabites, summons the seer Balaam, that he might come and lay curses to the destruction of the Israelites. And he set out, but on the road, a divine angel having set upon him, the donkey on which Balaam rode, perceiving the divine spirit, would not go forward nor yield to the blows, but speaking in human voice by the divine will, called his master unjust for laying blows upon it and not understanding that it was hindered by God from serving the purpose to which he was hastening. And while he was troubled at the human voice, the angel appeared and said that it was he himself who was hindering the road for the beast; and though Balaam wished to turn back, he urged him to go further forward, and to say whatever should be inspired in him by God. And he comes to Balak, and being brought to a mountain, having offered seven bulls and as many rams as whole burnt offerings, when he saw a turning of events signified, not only did he not curse the Hebrews, but, divinely inspired, he blessed them and their whole race and praised them in song. And when Balak was vexed at this, Balaam said, "It does not rest with us, O king, to be silent or to speak about such things, but whenever the spirit of God takes hold of us, it sends forth through us such utterances as it wishes. But since I wish to gratify you, an altar must again be prepared, and victims." So he sacrifices again, and falling upon his face he foretold what sufferings would come upon kings and what upon cities. But Balak sends Balaam away dishonored. Then he sends the maidens against the Israelites, according to the counsel of Balaam, by whom the young men of the Hebrews were captivated and consorted with them, so that now the transgression spread through the whole army, the young men, out of love of the Midianite women, sacrificing to their gods and tasting unaccustomed foods. But Moses, leading the people to an assembly, said that the young men were doing things unworthy of themselves and of their fathers, and tried to set them right. But Zimri, who was the chief of the tribe of Simeon, and dwelt with a Midianite woman and loved her madly, behaved insolently toward Moses, and swore that he would never leave the woman. And Phinehas, the son of the high priest Eleazar, in great anguish did not cease striking the Midianite woman and Zimri with the sword until he had killed both of them. And other young men too, who cared for virtue, imitating him, slew those of the young men who had transgressed with foreign women. So there perished men not fewer than fourteen thousand. From this Moses, provoked against the Midianites, sent out an army, appointing as its commander Phinehas. And when the battle was joined, their kings fall, being five, and a very great multitude. And the Hebrews plundered their country, and destroying the inhabitants together with the women, they left alive only the maidens, numbered at thirty-two thousand, whom Moses distributed among the priests and the Levites and the people. And being now an old man, he appointed as his successor Joshua the son of Nun, at God's command.

19. The tribes of Gad and Reuben and the half of Manasseh asked Moses to allot to them the land of the Amorites. But he called them cowards, men unwilling to share with their kinsmen in the battle against the Canaanites. They, however, replied that this was not so, but that, abounding in a multitude of cattle, they wished to leave these in that country, which was good for the feeding of four-footed beasts, so that they themselves might set out unencumbered with their kinsmen to the struggles. Moses approved this and allotted them the Amorite land on such terms.
And when a certain man of the tribe of Manasseh had died, leaving only daughters, Moses, being asked whose his inheritance should be, answered, "If the maidens marry men of their own tribe, let them go with the inheritance to those men; but if they be betrothed to men of another tribe, let them leave the inheritance in their ancestral tribe." And so he ordained that each one's inheritance should remain within the tribes.
And when forty years had now passed, less thirty days, since the Israelites had gone out of Egypt, Moses, having gathered the people, being a hundred and twenty years old, announced to them his own end. And having exhorted them much, and given laws in books and the ordering of their commonwealth, and commanded them to make war against the Amalekites, and required of them an oath concerning the keeping of the laws, and spurred on the leader Joshua to make war against the Canaanites, he said, "Behold, I go to our forefathers; for God has shown me this day of my coming to them."
