And the multitude wept, and their lamentation was inconsolable and so great that even Moses himself was overcome by the emotion and shed tears. And as he went to where he was to vanish from sight, all followed, beating their breasts. But he, signaling with his hand to those at a distance, bade them remain, and only the council of elders escorted him, and the high priest Eleazar and the general Joshua, until he came to the mountain Nebo, to the peak of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho; from there the Lord showed him the land that the sons of Israel were to inherit, saying to him, "See this with your eyes, but into it you shall not enter." And coming to this mountain, which was high, he sent away the council of elders, but while speaking with Eleazar and Joshua, a cloud suddenly enfolded him and he became invisible. And they have written in the sacred books that he died, lest, on account of the surpassing greatness of his virtue, some should dare to say that he had been made a god. He lived in all a hundred and twenty years, of which he ruled the third part, less one month. And they mourned him for thirty days. These things Josephus says; but the book of Deuteronomy contains, near its end, thus, word for word: "And Moses, the servant of the Lord, died, and no one knows his end to this day."
Now when the mourning had abated, Joshua sends spies to Jericho, and having summoned the chiefs of the tribes of Reuben and Gad and Manasseh, he reminded them of their agreements with Moses. And with fifty thousand foot soldiers following him, he advanced to the Jordan. And the spies sent to Jericho, coming there, observed the whole city, but being made known to the king of the country, they are reported; and he at once commanded that they be seized. But when the woman with whom they had taken refuge, called Rahab, learned of the approach of those seeking the men, she hid the spies, having placed bundles of flax over them, and to those seeking she said that those unknown men had dined with her before sunset and had departed. And so, the woman having deceived them, they set out, each in a different direction, pursuing the men. But Rahab bade the men go to their own people and remember her and pay her a recompense when they had become masters of the land of the Canaanites. And they acknowledged that they were grateful, and commanded that, when the city should be taken, she should shut up her possessions and her household in her lodging, and hang a scarlet cord before the doors, that the house might be recognized and preserved. And they were brought safely to their own people and made known what they had done. And though the Jordan was flowing in flood, Joshua thus brought the Hebrews across it. The priests went before, carrying the ark, then the Levites bearing the tabernacle, and the people followed these. And when the stream of the river was cut off as the priests first stepped in, all crossed over in confidence. And the priests stood in the midst until the multitude had crossed; then they too came out, letting the stream flow free. And ten stadia before Jericho

20. they encamp. And Joshua, having set up an altar from the stones that each of the chiefs of the tribes had taken up from the depth of the Jordan at his command, sacrificed upon it and kept the festival of the Passover. At that time too the manna had failed them, after they had used it for forty years; for now they had abundance from the country of all that they needed. And on the first day of the festival Joshua undertook the siege of Jericho, conducting it thus. The priests, carrying the ark, went round the wall, sounding seven horns, and the council of elders followed; then they returned to the camp. And this they did for six days. But on the seventh, when they had done the same and gone round seven times, the wall fell down, and the people, entering, killed all and burned the city. Only Rahab, with her household, the spies saved, since she had hung a scarlet cord before the house. And Joshua gave her fields as a gift and held her in honor. And against those who should wish to raise up the city again he laid curses, that he who laid the foundations should be deprived of his firstborn child, and he who completed it should be bereaved of his youngest. And a great quantity of silver and gold is gathered from the city, and all was dedicated to God as being the firstfruits of their successes; for it had been forbidden to all to appropriate anything from this. But a certain Achar, of the tribe of Judah, finding a garment woven with gold and a lump of gold weighing two hundred shekels, made these his own, having buried them in his tent. After this, when a battle was joined, the Hebrews are routed and thirty-six of their men fall. This grieved the multitude greatly. And Joshua, falling upon his face, prayed to God. And being informed by an oracle that a theft of the consecrated goods had occurred, he committed the judgment to the lot. And when the lot fell upon Achar, he confesses the theft and brings forth the stolen things. And he is killed with stones, together with his household; and Joshua besieges Ai and takes it.
But the Gibeonites and their neighbors, who belonged to the Canaanites, fearing that they would suffer the same as the people of Jericho and Ai, send an embassy to Joshua, saying that they dwelt very far off and had no kinship with the Canaanites, and seeking that the Israelites make a treaty and a covenant of friendship with them. So Joshua made friendship with them. But learning afterward that they were of the race of the Canaanites, he charged them with the deceit. They, however, said that they had done this of necessity, fearing destruction. And Joshua, that he might not transgress the oath, appoints them public servants. So says Josephus; but the book of Joshua records that they appointed them hewers of wood and drawers of water for the whole congregation and for the altar of God. And when the king of Jerusalem attacked the Gibeonites on account of their treaty with the Hebrews, Joshua allies himself with them and routs the enemy, and pursued them as they fled. At that time too hail greater than usual and thunderbolts fell from heaven upon the enemy, and the day was lengthened, God having stopped the course of the sun at the entreaty of Joshua, that the enemy might not escape with the coming on of night. And the kings too are caught, hidden in a certain cave, and all are killed. And Joshua returned again to the hill country of Canaan, and having wrought a great slaughter of those in it and taken spoil, he came to the camp at Gilgal. And the place of the camp was called Gilgal, since the Israelites now recognized themselves to be free of the Egyptians and of the hardship in the wilderness; for the Hebrews call freedom "galgala." And the Canaanites about Lebanon and those in the plains make war upon them, allied with the Palestinians. And their army was three hundred thousand foot soldiers, and ten thousand horsemen and thirty thousand chariots. And when God had promised victory, a strong battle takes place, so that the whole army of the enemy, except a few, was destroyed, and the kings too fell.

21. Now the fifth year had already passed, and no longer was any one of the Canaanites left. And Joshua sets up the tabernacle at the city of Shiloh, until it should be possible to build them a temple. And gathering the people to Shiloh, he reckoned up the cities that had been taken and how many armies of the enemy had been destroyed, and that thirty-one of their kings had been killed. But the cities still left, he said, required a long siege on account of their strength, and he asked to release to their homes those from across the Jordan who had set out with them. And summoning those of the two tribes and the half, who were fifty thousand, he permitted them to go to their allotments. And they, crossing the Jordan, set up an altar on the bank. This caused a tumult among the multitude of the Israelites. So they send against them ten of the honored men and Phinehas, charging them concerning the altar. But they said that they had not set up the altar for any innovation, but as a token to those who came after of their kinship with you; for they acknowledged one God, common to all the Hebrews. When they had said these things, Phinehas and those with him returned to Joshua. And Joshua, having allotted the lands to the multitude, passed his time at Shechem. And being now very old and about to die, he made an exhortation to the multitude, and ended his life, having lived a hundred and ten years, of which he passed forty with Moses, and after his death, leading the army, twenty-five. And the high priest Eleazar too dies, leaving the high-priesthood to his son Phinehas.
After this the Canaanites, hoping to prevail over the race of the Hebrews now that Joshua was dead, made war against them, entrusting the command to King Adonibezek. The name means "Lord of Bezek"; for "Adoni" in Hebrew means "lord." And the two tribes, that of Judah and that of Simeon, engaging the Canaanites, rout them and capture Adonibezek and maim him. And they took many cities, and the lower city of Jerusalem, and killed the inhabitants; but the siege of the upper city was difficult, both by the nature of the ground and by the strength of the walls. And having taken Hebron too, they put all to the sword, and gave it to Caleb for an inheritance, as Moses had commanded. And to the descendants of Jethro, who were kinsmen of Moses, they allotted land, because, leaving their fatherland, they had accompanied the people of the Hebrews in the wilderness. And the tribes of Judah and Simeon, having greatly prospered, laid down their arms. But the tribe of Ephraim, besieging Bethel, accomplished nothing. And having seized one of the men of the city, they gave him pledges that, if he handed over his fatherland, they would save both him and his kindred. And so he, having thus betrayed it, is saved with his household, while they, killing the inhabitants, held the city. And the Benjamites, since the city of Jerusalem had fallen to their lot, laid tribute upon the inhabitants, permitting them to live, contrary to the divine ordinances. And the other tribes did likewise.

22. Now when those of Israel were prospering, luxury corrupted them, and they transgressed the divine laws and were disinclined toward labor, and the aristocracy failed, and the council of elders was no longer appointed. Whence a terrible sedition seizes them from such a cause as this. A man, a Levite, taking along his wife, who was from Bethlehem, was going home. And as it was now evening, he is lodged as a guest with a certain old man in Gibeah, a city of the tribe of Benjamin. But certain young men of Gibeah, having seen the woman, came demanding her; and when the old man would not give her, they threatened to kill him. And he offered them his own daughter, that those lodged with him might not suffer any violence. But they, seizing the woman, departed, and having sated themselves with her through the whole night, they let her go at the break of day. And she, cast down by the night's hardship and by shame before her husband and by grief, perished. And her husband, dividing the dead woman into twelve parts, sent a part to each tribe, teaching them both the outrage and those responsible for the calamity. So they send to Gibeah, demanding the surrender of those who had transgressed; but they would not give them up. And the tribes made war against them, and twice, when they engaged, the Israelites are defeated. Then through Phinehas the high priest they pray to God, and so, engaging the Benjamites, they prevailed, so that all fell except six hundred, who fled to the neighboring mountains. And the Israelites burned Gibeah and put to the sword the women and children, and on the other cities too they did the like. And the inhabitants of Jabesh of Gilead, because it had not allied with them, they slay, with women and children, except four hundred maidens, whom they gave to the survivors of the Benjamites, that they might have them as wives, taking pity on their calamity. And they considered how the remaining two hundred too might be provided with women; for they had previously sworn, on account of the outrage, that no one would give a daughter in marriage to a Benjamite. And on consideration it seemed good to them not themselves to give, on account of the oath, but that it should be permitted to the Benjamites, by seizing maidens, to take them as wives for themselves, they neither hindering nor encouraging. And so it seemed good to them about these things, and the Benjamites brought to deed what had seemed good.
Now, the Israelites having long before ceased from fighting, the Canaanites despised them and took cities from them. And those of the tribe of Dan fled to the mountain, and from there migrated to the interior. But against the Israelites, who had taken on the customs of the Canaanites and despised their own commonwealth, the Divine was angered. So the king of the Assyrians, Cushan-rishathaim, makes war against them and lays heavy tributes upon them, by which they were oppressed for eight years. Then a man of action of the tribe of Judah, called Othniel, having gathered to himself a few men, by a divine oracle destroys the garrison of the Assyrians among them. And when more had afterward been gathered, having conquered the Assyrians in battle, he drove them off, and for this was chosen to rule the multitude and to judge the people. He, having held the rule for fifty years, departed life. And the Israelites, being without a ruler and despising the Divine, were made subject by Aiglom the king of the Moabites and were charged with annual contributions. He, having built a palace in Jericho, ill-treated them in many ways for eighteen years. But a certain young Benjamite, Aoth by name—Josephus says this man was called Judas—daring and strong, becomes familiar with Aiglom, and continually frequented his presence, flattering the man and ingratiating himself. This man, once bringing gifts to Aiglom with two servants, carried a small dagger concealed. And as the day was now at its middle and the guards had withdrawn to themselves, finding him alone, he goes in as a familiar, and taking him by himself, as though to converse with him about something more secret, he strikes him mortally with the dagger and kills him. And going to the people of Jericho, he persuades them to lay claim to liberty. And they armed themselves, while those about Aiglom, finding him dead, turn to flight and are destroyed as they are pursued. And so the Hebrews are freed from the slavery of the Moabites, and the rule of the multitude was entrusted to Aoth. He, having led the people for eighty years, ended his life. And after him Megar, the son of Dinach, ruling, died in the first year of his rule, having struck down many of the foreigners.

23. And when the people of the Hebrews transgressed the divine laws, God was angered. And Sisera, the commander-in-chief of Jabin the king of Canaan, attacking them, ill-treated them greatly and subjected them to tributes; and they were thus for twenty years. But a certain prophetess Deborah—the name means "bee"—supplicated God on behalf of the people. And God consented, and bids them choose as general Barak; and this means "lightning" in the language of the Hebrews. The man was of the tribe of Naphtali. And Deborah urged Barak to go against the enemy with ten thousand men, since God commanded this. But he demanded that she too share the command. The woman is persuaded, and when battle was joined for them with the ten thousand against Sisera, much rain pours down and hail breaks forth, and these were driven by the wind against the face of the enemy and darkened their sight, and from this they bent to flight. And Sisera too, fleeing, took refuge with a certain woman, asking her to hide him; the woman was named Jael. And she receives him and gives him milk to drink, and he, having drunk, fell asleep. And while he slept, Jael set upon him, and driving a nail through his temple, pinned him to the ground, and shows the dead enemy to those about Barak. And Barak, making war also against Jabin the king of Canaan, killed him and razed his city. And having been general for thirty years, he dies, Deborah also dying at the same time. Then the Midianites, with the Amalekites and Arabs, routed the Israelites in battle. And while they attacked them for seven years there was famine and lack of necessities, and they prayed to God. And Gideon, of the tribe of Manasseh, was secretly beating sheaves of grain in the winepress, and he sees one standing by him in the form of a young man, calling him a friend of God and blessed. And he, in irony, said that the proof of his blessedness was his using the winepress instead of a threshing-floor. And the young man exhorted him to take courage and to hasten for the liberty of his fellow tribesmen. And Gideon begged the one who appeared not to depart from there, and going in he brought a sacrifice. And the angel commanded him to set it by the rock; and touching the rock with his rod, he kindled a fire of its own accord and consumed the sacrifice. Then Gideon asked God that dew should come upon the fleece, and it came; and again he asked that dew should come upon all the ground, but dryness upon the fleece, and so it was. So Gideon is persuaded, and with ten thousand armed himself against the enemy. Then by command of God he leads them all at midday to the river, and taking with himself those who lapped while drinking and drank with haste, as though fearful—these were three hundred—he set out for the war, and left the rest behind. And by night, taking one of the soldiers, he went to the camp of the enemy. And he hears one of the enemy relating to his tent-mate that he had seemed to see in his sleep a barley loaf rolling through the camp, which overthrew the tent of the king and those of the army; and the other judged that the dream signified the destruction of the army, likening to a barley loaf Gideon and those with him, on account of their fewness and weakness. Hearing this, Gideon took courage, and returning he commanded his men to be at their arms, and dividing the army into three hundreds, he ordered each to carry an empty jar and a lighted torch and a ram's horn, and at the fourth watch of the night he led them out against the enemy. And being now near them, they sounded the horns and broke the jars, and with the torches they rushed forward shouting. These things struck terror into the enemy, and some were killed by the enemy themselves, while the greater part were destroyed by one another, since it was night, and nearly all perished, and two of their kings, Oreb and Zeeb. And those of the leaders and the army who were left, fleeing, are caught by Gideon and those with him, and all fell. And Gideon held the rule for forty years, and died an old man, leaving from various wives seventy legitimate sons, and one from a concubine, called Abimelech. He, having killed all his brothers except one, Jotham, who fled, set up a tyranny. But the people, rising against Abimelech, drive him out of the city of Shechem. And he, aided by one of the Shechemites, takes the city by treachery and slays the Shechemites of full age, and razes the city. And he marched against Thebes, another city, and took it by assault. But the multitude ran together into one great tower, which was in the middle of the city. And as Abimelech drew near to its gates, a woman threw down a fragment of a millstone from above upon his head and killed him. And the rule of the Hebrews was entrusted to Jair, who was of the tribe of Manasseh; and he, having directed the rule for twenty-two years, died. Then the Ammonites with the Palestinians next plundered the country. And while the Ammonites were ravaging Gilead, the inhabitants chose Jephthah as leader. He, being about to engage the enemy, made a vow that, if he should conquer, he would sacrifice whatever first met him as he returned. And engaging, he conquers; but as he returned, his little daughter met him, who was his only child and still a virgin. And he lamented aloud, but, that he might not break his promise, he sacrificed the girl and offered her as a whole burnt offering. And when those of the tribe of Ephraim were angry with him because he had not taken them along to the war against the Ammonites, since he could not persuade them with apologies, he killed many of them who fought with him. And having held the leadership for six years, he ended his life. And the rule is taken up by Amesa, who was of the tribe of Judah, and having judged Israel for seven years, he died. And after him Labdon, coming forth from the tribe of Ephraim, was appointed leader, and died an old man, having ruled eight years.

24. Then the Palestinians prevailed over the Israelites and held them tributary for forty years. At that time was born Samson—the name signifies "strength"—who set himself against the Palestinians; and the beginning of his life came about thus. Manoah, being of the tribe of Dan, dwelt with a barren wife and asked God that a child be given to them. So once, when the woman was alone, there appeared a young man, great and fair, bringing the good news of the birth of a child, and he commanded her not to drink wine or strong drink, nor to cut the hair of the child; for he said that the child would be a Nazirite to the Lord—that is, holy—and that Israel would be saved through him from the hand of the foreigners. And she announced these things to her husband. And he prayed to God that the one who had appeared to his wife might appear to him also. So again the angel came to the woman; but Manoah was again absent; and the woman begged him to await the coming of her husband. And Manoah, coming, asked the angel what they should do when the child was born. And he said, "He shall not drink wine or strong drink, and shall eat nothing unclean, and his hair shall not be shaved." And Manoah sought to learn the name of the one speaking with him, but he said that it was wonderful, and was silent. And Manoah, bringing a kid, sacrificed it and offered loaves. And the angel commanded him to set the flesh and the loaves upon the rock, and when they were set he touches them with his rod, and a fire, kindled from there, consumed them, and through the flame the angel went up to heaven, while Manoah and his wife looked on. So after these things the child is born to them and is named Samson, and he grew, and the spirit of the Lord went along with him. And seeing in Thamna, a city of the Palestinians, a girl of the foreigners, he falls in love with the maiden. And though his parents deprecated the marriage with a foreign woman, he prevailed to marry her. And while frequenting the parents of the girl, he meets a lion, and having nothing for defense, he crushed the beast with his hands, and turning aside from the road he threw it into the brushwood. And after some days, going again to his betrothed, he found a swarm of bees gathered in the mouth of the lion. And taking from there a honeycomb, he ate it and brought some to his father and mother. And going to the foreigners, he sets a riddle for the thirty young men who were feasting with him at the wedding; and he agreed, if they should find the solution within seven days, to give each of them a linen cloth and a robe, but if they could not solve the riddle, he demanded that a robe and a linen cloth be given to him by each. And when the young men had agreed, he put forward the question, saying, "Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong, sweetness." And they, unable to perceive the riddle, begged the girl to learn it from the man and report it to them. And Samson, when the girl entreated him to tell her the meaning of the riddle, at first resisted, but when she wept, he told her the whole; and she reported it to the young men. And on the seventh day they said to Samson, "What is sweeter than honey, or what is stronger than a lion?" So Samson was angered, and gave the young men what he had promised, but renounced the marriage. And the father gave the woman to another. And Samson, provoked at this, having caught three hundred foxes, tied lighted torches to their tails and let them loose upon the fields of the Palestinians at the onset of summer, and thus burned up their crops and their vines. And the Palestinians in return burned and consumed with fire the woman who had been his wife and her relatives. And Samson, having killed many of the foreigners, settled himself on a rock; but they made war against the Israelites, saying, "If you wish to be guiltless, give us Samson into our hands." And three thousand armed men went to the rock. And Samson, coming down willingly, gave himself up to his fellow tribesmen, and they handed him over bound to the Palestinians. But he, breaking the bonds and snatching up the jawbone of an ass thrown down somewhere there, killed a thousand of the foreigners with it, and routed the rest. Whence from that time the place was called Siagon ("Jawbone"). Then he thirsted so as to faint from thirst, and he wept, praying to God. And God sent up a spring of water from the cleft that Samson had made by throwing the jawbone to the ground. And he went to Gaza. But the men of Gaza set an ambush for him, and that he might not escape their notice as he went out, they shut the gates of the city. But he, rising about midnight, hoisted upon his shoulders the gates and their posts and the doorframes and carried them up to the summit of the mountain and set them down there. And falling in love with a Palestinian courtesan called Delilah, he consorted with her; and the chief men of the foreigners made many promises to the woman, if she should learn from Samson what was the cause of his strength and report it to them. And she went after the man in various ways, seeking to know whence came such great strength to him; but he, feigning now one cause, now another, told the woman. And the woman, testing his words, found them to be deceptions. But as she pressed and entreated him more warmly, he revealed to her the secret, saying that by the command of God he let his hair grow, since God had commanded not to cut it, and that in this lay his strength. The woman cuts his hair while he slept and hands him over weak to the enemy. And they put out the man's eyes, and he who had once been fearful became a plaything for them. But as time went on, his hair grew again and his strength returned. And when the Palestinians were holding a drinking-feast, and the rulers and nobles were feasting together in a house supported by pillars, Samson too was brought to be made sport of, and a young boy led him by the hand. And there was gathered by the house a multitude of men and women, about three thousand, that they might see Samson abused. And he, being mocked and struck, says to the one leading him by the hand, "Bring me to the pillars, that I may lean upon them, since I need to rest." And grasping the two pillars, he pulled the house down upon himself, and he himself and all those in the house perished. And such was the end of this man, who had judged the people of the Hebrews for twenty years.

25. No longer did judges lead Israel, but the high priest Eli presided over them; in his time there was a famine, and a certain man of Bethlehem called Abimelech migrated with his wife and two sons into Moab on account of the famine. So he takes Moabite wives for his sons. Within ten years, however, both Abimelech and his sons died, and there were left as widows both Naomi, the wife of Abimelech, and the two wives of his sons, Orpah and Ruth. And Naomi returned to her fatherland, and of her daughters-in-law Orpah, being entreated by her mother-in-law, remained among the Moabites, but Ruth departed with Naomi. And when they had now come to Bethlehem, Boaz, who was a kinsman of Abimelech, received them as guests. And when the woman was addressed by name by the citizens, she said, "Call me not Naomi but Mara"—for "Naomi" means "good fortune," but "Mara" means "grief and bitterness"—"for I went out full and returned empty." And as it was harvest time, Ruth went out, by the counsel of her mother-in-law, to glean in the field of Boaz. And he, seeing the girl and learning who she was, permitted her to reap what she could and to keep it, and commanded the farm-overseer to provide her a meal. And she, having received barley meal from him, kept it for her mother-in-law, and went away late, carrying also the barley she had gathered, and related to her the things she had from Boaz. And again she went out with the maidservants of Boaz. And Naomi resolved to lay Ruth beside him, and sends her daughter-in-law, having instructed her to fall asleep at the feet of the man while he slept on the threshing-floor. And so she did, but Boaz, perceiving about midnight, asked who she was. And learning, he then kept quiet, but at dawn, waking Ruth, he commanded her to go to her mother-in-law, and said, "I myself will ask the one who is a nearer kinsman to you, and if he wishes to take you, you shall go to that man, but if he declines, you shall lawfully dwell with me." So the woman went away and reported everything to Naomi. And Boaz called together before the council of elders Ruth and the kinsman, and said to him, "Do you hold the inheritance of Abimelech our kinsman and of his sons?" And when he had agreed to hold it according to the laws by right of kinship, Boaz said, "Then one must not remember the laws by halves, but in all things do according to them. It remains that you must also marry the wife of Mahlon, the son of Abimelech, that you may raise up seed for the kinsman." But he declined, yielding to him both the inheritance and the woman. So, according to the law, before the council of elders Ruth loosed the sandal of that man and spat in his face. And so Boaz took her, and she bore him Obed—which in Greek is interpreted "serving." And from Obed comes Jesse, and from him David, who reigned over those of Israel and left the rule to his children, which endured for twenty-one generations.
And while Eli the high priest, as has already been related, was leading the people, his two sons Hophni and Phinehas were pestilent, transgressing in all things, and not turning back when their father exhorted them. And God, angered on account of their transgressions, through Samuel, who was still a child, made known to Eli what he himself and his children and his house would suffer. Now Samuel was the son of Elkanah, a Levite man, with whom dwelt two wives, of whom the one was named Hannah and the other Peninnah. And to one there were children from Elkanah, but Hannah was without offspring. And when the man came with both wives to Shiloh and had sacrificed, since it was a time of feasting and Peninnah rejoiced with her children, Hannah, because she was alone, wept for herself, and running to the tabernacle of God, prayed to the Lord to grant her offspring, vowing to consecrate the firstborn to God. And as she lingered in her prayers, Eli, sitting before the tabernacle, supposed her to be drunk and sent her away. But she said, "I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, lord, but being in anguish on account of my childlessness I have wasted away." And the priest said to her, "Go, and may God grant you your request." And returning home with her husband, she conceives and bears Samuel—one might call him "asked of God." And when the child had grown, she brings him to Eli, according to the vow, to be reared for God, letting his hair grow and dwelling in the sanctuary and using water for drink. And being now twelve years old, he prophesied. And once, while he slept, God called him by name. And he went to the high priest, supposing that he was perhaps called by him. And this happened three times. And Eli, perceiving that the call was from God, said to Samuel, "If you are called again, say, 'Behold I am here, Lord.'" And when the child had done so, the one who called said to him that there would be a heavy calamity for the Israelites, and that the sons of Eli would die together and the priesthood would pass over to the house of Eleazar. And Samuel was unwilling to disclose the words to the priest, but, constrained by oaths, he reported everything just as he had heard.

26. From this the Palestinians make war against the Israelites, and were superior in the battle. And the people ask that the ark be brought to their aid. And when the ark was sent there with the sons of Eli, a battle was joined. And the Hebrews were defeated, and about thirty thousand fell, and the sons of the high priest, and the ark was taken by the enemy. And Eli the high priest was sitting upon a high seat, and learning of the battle and the slaughter of his sons and the capture of the ark, in great anguish he fell from his seat and died, being ninety years old, of which he had led Israel forty years. And the foreigners, having carried off the ark to the city of Azotus, dedicated it to Dagon—for so they called their god. And at dawn, entering the house of Dagon, they found the image lying before the ark upon the ground. And raising it up, they set it upon its former base. But when they found this happen often, and many times having set the idol upright, found it as often lying in the posture of one worshiping the ark, they were astounded and at a loss. Then a destruction fell upon the city and country of the Azotians—a disease among the people about the seat, which Josephus calls dysentery, and many died of it; and mice, springing up from the ground, ravaged the whole country. And at last the Azotians understood that the ark was the cause of their sufferings, and they send it to Ascalon; and those too suffered the like. And so the ark passed through five cities of the Palestinians, and to all became a cause of affliction. So the rulers of the five afflicted cities came together—of Gath and Ekron and Ascalon and Gaza and Azotus—and some counseled one thing about the ark, others another. And at last it seemed good to all to make five golden seats and as many golden mice and to place them upon the ark, and to make a new wagon and yoke to the wagon cows that had borne their first calves, but to keep back their calves, and to set the ark upon the wagon, and, having led the cows to a place where three roads met, to leave them, that it might rest with them to go whichever way they should set out: if they went straight toward the Israelites, they would believe that on account of the ark the evils were being brought upon them, and would not hinder their journey to those people; but if they went somewhere else, they would turn the cows and the wagon and what was on it back again. Having, then, accomplished what seemed good, they let the cows go, themselves following at a distance, that they might see the outcome. And they went straight toward the Hebrews and did not stop before they came to a great plain in Bethshemesh. So when the men of that village saw the ark, they hastened to it, and taking it down from the wagon, they sacrificed the cows and offered them as whole burnt offerings with the wood of which the wagon had been made. And seeing this, the Palestinians returned home. But those who touched the ark, not being priests, God in anger put to death. And the rest made known to the community of the Hebrews the things concerning the ark; and they, taking it, carry it away to Kiriath-jearim and deposit it in the house of Aminadab, who was of the tribe of Levi. And it remained there twenty years, but among the foreigners four months.
And Samuel the prophet, having now gained a great name and come to much glory, gathering the people, spoke to them about freedom and persuaded them to lay claim to it. Learning this, the Palestinians come unexpectedly upon the Hebrews and terrified them, so that they ran to Samuel, saying that their safety was despaired of unless he himself asked for them the aid from God. And he exhorted them to take courage, and assured them that God would help them, and having sacrificed a lamb, he prayed to God. And before the sacred flame had consumed the sacrifice, the enemy attacked the Hebrews, supposing they would more easily prevail over them as unarmed. But when the earth was shaken by God with an earthquake, and thunders broke forth and lightnings flashed, the enemy fell into cowardice and turned to flight. And Samuel and the multitude pursued after them and destroyed many, and no longer after this blow did they make war against the Israelites, but Samuel even recovered for the Hebrews the country that they had taken. And he judged the people and ruled over them.

27. And being now grown old, he distributed to his sons the leadership of the people and the office of judging. The name of the elder was Joel, and of the younger Abiah. But they did not walk in the ways of their father, but, turning aside, betrayed justice for gifts and gave their judgments for bribes. And the people, on account of this, gathering to Samuel, said, "Since you are not able to preside over us by reason of age, make us a king, who shall both lead the nation and make war against the enemy." And while Samuel grieved at this, God said to him, "It is not you the people have rejected, but me. Hearken, then, to them, and whomever I shall point out to you, anoint him as king." And gathering the Hebrews, Samuel set forth that he would appoint them a king, but foretold that they would repent and would ask of God a deliverance from kings. But they persisted, seeking a king, and asked him not to be concerned about what was to come. And the prophet said, "Go now, and when I learn whom God gives you as king, I will send for you."
Now there was a certain Benjamite, Kish by name, who, having lost his donkeys, sent his son, who was tall and fair and called Saul, in search of the donkeys, with one of his servants. And he, having gone about and sought and not found them, came to Armathaim, to Samuel, to inquire about the donkeys. So God reveals to Samuel that this is he whom He wishes to reign over the people of the Hebrews. So when Saul asked about the donkeys, Samuel said that they had been recovered, and having lodged Saul, he sent him forth at dawn, and going outside the city with him and taking the young man aside alone, he pours oil upon his head. And kissing him, he said, "The Lord has anointed you ruler over his people Israel, and let this be the sign of the anointing: that two men shall meet you about the tomb of Rachel, bringing you the good news of the finding of the donkeys." And he told him other signs of the truth, and that he would prophesy when he came to Gabatha among the prophets there, and he commanded him to come to Gilgal when he should be summoned by him. And then he gathered the people and bade the tribes cast lots, that it might be shown from which the one who was to reign would be. So the lot fell upon Benjamin, then upon the family of Mattari. And when the family had been allotted man by man, the lot fell upon Saul. And as, when sought, he was not found, Samuel is informed by God where he was hidden, and having him brought, set him in the midst. And he was a head taller than all and surpassing all in the stature of his body. And the prophet said to the multitude, "This man the Lord has anointed for you as king, to whom there is none like among you all." And the people shouted approval and said, "Long live the king." So, when Saul had thus become king, many attended him as king and honored him as was fitting, but many despised and mocked him.
And after a month Nahash the king of the Ammonites makes war against Jabesh-gilead, saying that he would not otherwise spare the men unless they gave him the right eye of each to put out. And they asked for a respite of seven days; and receiving it, they send messengers to Gabaa. And when those there heard the words of the Ammonite, they wept; but Saul was greatly angered, and taking two oxen, he cut them in pieces and sent them into all the territory of Israel, threatening to do likewise to those who would not march out with him against the Ammonites. And when the people had run together, he numbered them and found seven hundred thousand. And the spirit of the Lord leaped upon Saul, and he prophesied, saying that on the morrow there would be deliverance for the men of Jabesh. And rising, he himself and the people marched all night, and about the morning watch he came upon the Ammonites, dividing the army into three parts. And surrounding them, he killed many, and the king Nahash himself, and turned the survivors to flight; and invading their country and taking very much spoil, he returned in splendor. So no longer was he held in low esteem by any, but he was renowned for his courage and honored even by those who had formerly mocked him. And Samuel, gathering the people again, proclaims Saul king a second time, anointing him again with the oil. So the commonwealth of the Hebrews passed from an aristocracy into a kingship; for in the time of Moses and Joshua they were governed as an aristocracy, then for eighteen years they continued without a ruler, and afterward they were ruled by those called judges, entrusting to the best man the judging and management of all affairs.

28. And when Samuel adjured the people to say if he had done any wrong to them, all cried out that he had presided over the nation justly and well. And he answered them, "Know that you have greatly sinned in asking a king for yourselves, and by this you have provoked God to anger. And this shall be a sign to you, that in the height of summer there shall come a storm." And according to the word of the prophet there were thunders and lightnings, and hail came down, so that fear fell upon the people and they entreated Samuel to come and reconcile God to them, since they had sinned.
And while the Palestinians were subduing the Hebrews and taking away their arms and forbidding them to use iron, Saul, going down to Gilgal, urged the people to rise up against the Palestinians for their freedom. But they were cautious on account of the multitude of the enemy. And the king called Samuel to him. And he promised to come after six days, and to sacrifice on the seventh, that so they might engage the foreigners. But Saul, seeing the people slipping away and abandoning him, sacrificed. And hearing that Samuel was now approaching, he went out to meet him. But he said, "What is this you have done, transgressing my command? Know, then, that your kingdom shall not stand, but the Lord shall seek a man after his own heart." And Samuel withdrew, but Saul and Jonathan his son came to Gabaa with six hundred soldiers. And the foreigners, divided into three parts, plundered the country of the Israelites. And Saul and Jonathan and Ahiah the high priest, seeing from a height what was being done, and not strong enough to defend on account of the fewness of their men, were grieved. But Jonathan, saying nothing to his father, went down from the hill with only his armor-bearer and said, "Let us attack the camp of the foreigners, and if they say to us, 'Stand off,' we will not go up to them, but if they say, 'Come up to us,' we must reckon the word a token of victory for us." And they set out for the camp of the enemy. And the foreigners said to them, "Come up to us, and we will make known to you a matter." This put courage into Jonathan; and withdrawing from there, he crept up from another side with his attendant and came upon the enemy while they slept. And they kill about twenty, and into the rest they put cowardice; who, thrown into confusion and fleeing, were destroyed by one another. And Saul, seeing the camp of the enemy thrown into confusion, and perceiving that his son was absent together with his armor-bearer, himself also attacks the disordered enemy; and those who before, out of fear, had hidden, taking courage, joined the king. And pursuing the enemy he kept killing them. So he laid a curse upon his own men, that if any one, ceasing from the slaughter of the enemy, should eat before night stopped them, he should die. And in the pursuit they came to a certain wood, in which there was a beehive, and Jonathan, taking a honeycomb, ate it; for he had not heard the curse of his father. And Saul, wishing to attack the camp of the enemy, asked God through the high priest whether He would grant victory. And when God did not reveal it, he sought the cause, and said, "I swear by God himself that I will kill the one who has sinned, even if it be Jonathan my son." And when they cast lots, the lot fell upon Jonathan. And he, being examined about the sin, said he was conscious of nothing in himself except that "yesterday, not knowing the curse, I tasted a honeycomb in the pursuit." And hearing this, his father swore that he would kill him. But the people swore in turn that they would not allow the author of the victory to die, and snatching him away, they propitiated God with prayers. And Saul, having destroyed about sixty thousand of the Palestinians, returned. And he subdues the Ammonites and Moabites and Palestinians and Idumaeans and Amalekites, and the king of Suba, and delivered Israel from the hand of the foreigners.

29. Now Saul had three sons, Jonathan and Ishvi and Malchishua, and two daughters, Merob and Michal; and he had as commander-in-chief Abner, the son of Ner, his kinsman.
And Samuel said to Saul that God commanded him to strike Amalek, and, when he had prevailed, to spare nothing—not women, not infants, not beasts of burden, not cattle—but to blot out his name from the earth. And Saul, engaging Amalek, conquers mightily and kills all, and takes captive also the king of the country, named Agag, and did not kill him, admiring him for his beauty and stature; and the choicest of the herds and flocks and the rest he kept for himself, forgetting the divine command. And Samuel, being informed by God, who said that He repented of having made Saul king, met the king. And he said that he gave thanks to God for granting him power over the enemy, and that he had done all that was commanded. And the prophet said, "I hear the bleating of beasts of burden and of other cattle. Whence are these?" And Saul said that the people had kept them for sacrifice to God, but that all the Amalekites had been destroyed except their king. To this Samuel said, "Since you have transgressed what was commanded you by God, know that you shall be deprived of the kingdom." And he confessed that he had sinned, and entreated the prophet to offer a propitiatory sacrifice. And as he withdrew, Saul lays hold of his cloak and tears it, forcing him to stay. And the prophet said, "So shall your kingdom be torn and given to a man righteous and good." And when the king still entreated, he is persuaded, and asks that Agag be brought, and when that man had been killed, at his command, he at once withdraws to Armathaim.
And God commands him to go to Jesse and to anoint with oil for king one of his sons, whomever He should point out to him. And going to Bethlehem and sacrificing, he called Jesse and his sons. And seeing the firstborn, tall and fair, he supposed that God favored him. But God said, "Look not upon his appearance, nor upon the greatness of his body; for man looks upon the face, but God upon the heart." And when the other sons of Jesse had passed by, God favored none of them. And Samuel said, "The Lord has not chosen among these, and if there is yet one remaining, let him come." And Jesse said, "There is still left the youngest, tending the flock." So the prophet commanded that he be called. And when David came, being called—a ruddy youth with fair eyes and otherwise fair—God reveals to Samuel that this was the one to be anointed. And he, taking the horn of oil, anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And he went away to Armathaim. And a divine spirit leaped upon David, but departed from Saul, and an evil spirit pursued him, choking and tormenting the man. So it seemed good that there should stand by the king one who knew how to play the harp, that when the demon fell upon him and troubled him, he might play upon the harp and lull the disturbance. So he sends for David as such a one; and the young man was greatly loved by the king, and became his armor-bearer. And when the evil spirit came upon the king, David sang over him, and it departed, and Saul came back to himself.
And the foreigners made war against the Israelites, and those of Israel set themselves against them. And in the space between the two armies a certain man of the foreigners stood—Goliath was his name—a powerful man towering above all, for his height was six cubits and a span, and his breastplate weighed five thousand shekels, and his spear was like a weaver's beam, and the head of the spear six hundred shekels; this man, standing in the midst, cried out to the sons of Israel, "Let one of you come down and stand against me; and if he strikes me, we will serve you, but if I lay him low, you shall be servants to us." And this he did for forty days. Now when Saul had sent David back to Jesse, his father sent him to the camp to bring provisions to his brothers who were in the army; for three of the elder ones were following Saul. And when David came to his brothers, the foreigner Goliath again, as was his custom, challenged to single combat and reproached the Hebrews because none dared to engage him. And hearing these words, David was indignant and said to those present, "I will fight him in single combat." This was reported to the king, and to David, standing before him, he said, "You will not be able to go in battle against this uncircumcised man, for you are still a boy." And David said he took courage in God, who had strengthened him against the bear and against the lion when they came upon the flock and snatched the young, whom, he said, he pursued and recovered what had been snatched, and struck the beasts and killed them. In Him, he said, he took courage, that He would grant him to strike down the foreigner too and to take away the reproach from the sons of Israel. So he said this, and the king permitted him to go, and put his own arms upon him. But they were a burden to him, and he took them off, and taking up his staff and putting five stones in his pouch and carrying the sling in his hand, he set out against the foreigner. And he laughed at him and asked whether he came against a dog with a staff and stones. And David answered that he reckoned him worse than a dog. And he, angered, and boasting that he would give his flesh to the birds and the beasts, rushed upon him. But David, being quick and putting a stone in the sling, struck the enemy upon the forehead. And the blow was mighty, and the foreigner fell upon his face. And David, running and drawing his sword, cuts off the head of Goliath and strips off his arms. This put cowardice into the foreigners, and they turned to flight. And Saul leads his own army against them as they fled; and a great multitude of the Palestinians is killed, and more are wounded, and their camp is plundered. And David brings the head of Goliath to Saul, but dedicates the sword to God.

30. And as the army returned, the women met them, and dancing they sang that Saul had slain thousands, while the maidens answered in song that David had destroyed ten thousands. This stirred Saul to envy, and he said, "What is lacking to him but the kingdom?" And he looked askance at David. And when an evil spirit fell upon Saul, and David sang over him as was his custom, Saul threw his spear at him; and he did this twice. But David turned aside, for the Lord was with him. And the king, fearing him, made him a commander of a thousand, that going against the enemy he might be endangered. But he, with God as ally, prospered, and the people loved him, and the king's daughter Michal loved David. So her love was reported to the king, and he used the love as a handle for a plot. For he said that he would give him his daughter if he would bring him a hundred foreskins, supposing that he would fall fighting the foreigners. Learning this, David went with his men, and struck among the foreigners and brought Saul a hundred foreskins. (But Josephus says that David brought not a hundred foreskins, but six hundred heads of foreigners.) And he joins to him his daughter Michal. But seeing David both allied with God and beloved by the multitude, he feared still more, and plotted against him, and tried to kill him. So he commands his son Jonathan and his most trusted servants to do away with him. But Jonathan, loving David, reveals to him the command, and exhorts him to be on his guard, and promises to speak about him to his father and to disclose everything to him. And indeed he spoke and turned him to gentleness; for, changing his mind, Saul swore that he would do David no wrong. And Jonathan, having revealed this to David, brings him to the king, and he remained with him as before. And when the Palestinians stirred again and came against the Hebrews, David is sent by Saul to set himself against them, and returns with victory. But with the man's successes the envy against him grew in Saul. And when the evil spirit came upon him again and choked him, David was present, striking the harp and singing over him. And Saul, holding his spear, hurled it at David; but he, foreseeing it, turned aside and withdrew. And Saul sent guards by night to David's house, that he might kill him by day. But Michal his wife, learning this, let her husband down through a window, and he fled. And at dawn, when Saul sent for David, Michal, having prepared the bed as though someone lay in it, and having placed under the coverings the liver of a freshly slaughtered goat, so that by its movement the covering, being shaken, might give the appearance that someone lay upon the bed, brings in those who had been sent and says that the man is sick. And they reported it to Saul, and he commanded that he be brought to him on the bed. But those sent, going and lifting the covering of the bed, perceived the trick and reported it to the king. So David, having thus escaped death, came to Samuel at Armathaim and passed his time with him at Nabioth in Rama. So Saul sends there too those who should bring David. But they, going and finding an assembly of prophets, themselves also prophesied. Learning this, the king sends others, and when these too were likewise affected, he sent still others, and when the third group too had been seized by the spirit, he himself set out in anger, and drawing near, he himself also began to prophesy. At which time those present uttered the saying, "Is Saul too among the prophets?" And coming to where Samuel was, becoming as it were out of his mind and stripping off his clothing, he lay naked through a whole day and night.

31. And David fled from there and made known to Jonathan his father's design against him; but he disbelieved it. And David asked him to make trial of his father's intent and to disclose it to him as he waited outside the city. So Jonathan, bringing words to his father about David, and having learned that his father's purpose thirsted for the man's death, reports everything to him secretly in person, and urges him to save himself. And he adjured David to remember him, and, even should he chance to die, to show some kindness to his offspring. Saying this, Jonathan returned, and David, fleeing to Nob, comes to Abimelech the high priest. And he inquired how he came alone. And David said that something secret had been commanded him by the king, "and that no one might know of it, I am alone; and here he ordered me to meet with my servants." Saying this, he asked for loaves. And the high priest said he had none but the holy ones, and, "If you have kept yourselves from a woman, take these and eat." And he asked that a sword too be given him. But the high priest answered that he had no other weapon except the sword of Goliath, which David himself had dedicated to God. And taking these, David went away to Gath, to Achish the king of the foreigners. And being recognized for who he was and taking fright, he feigned madness and behaved and acted as one out of his mind. And so, escaping safe from the foreigners, he comes to the tribe of Judah, and hides in the cave of Adullam. There his brothers and his kindred came to him; then others too flowed together there, so that all became about four hundred. And he goes from there to the Moabites, and begs the king of Moab to let his parents dwell with him until matters concerning him should come to some end. And he is persuaded and receives Jesse and his household. And David went into the land of Judah, since Gad the prophet commanded this. But Saul, learning that a multitude had gathered to David, called together his friends and reproached them as taking his part. And a certain servant of Saul, a Syrian by race, Doeg by name, who had been present when the high priest gave the loaves to David and the sword of Goliath, standing then beside him, reported to the king that he had seen David come to the high priest and inquire of God through him and receive provisions and the sword. And the king, summoning the high priest, charged him with conspiracy with David. And he commanded the armed men standing by him to kill the high priest and all his kindred; but when they shrank from laying hands on those consecrated to God, he orders Doeg to do the killing. And he killed them all, three hundred and five in number, and struck their city, killing all of full age, sparing neither women nor infants nor any other age. But one son of the high priest alone escaped death, called Abiathar, who, fleeing to David, reported what had happened.
And when the foreigners had invaded Keilah and were plundering the country, David, at God's command, came upon them with the four hundred, and struck them and brought back all the spoil. But Saul sends a multitude of soldiers to do away with him there. And he went from Keilah into the wilderness. And Saul did not cease seeking to put him to death. And Jonathan came to David and encouraged him and exhorted him to have good hopes. And when David had taken refuge upon the rock in the wilderness of Maon, and Saul came upon him with a great multitude, David was in danger of being taken, had not a messenger come to Saul that the foreigners had attacked the country; for, leaving David, he set out against the enemy. Then it was reported to him that David was encamped in the wilderness of Gaddi, and taking three thousand he set out. And as he went he was troubled by his bowels. And there was a certain cave there, in which David and those with him were hidden farther within; into this Saul entered to relieve himself. And David was urged by those with him to kill Saul. But he was not persuaded; rather, he secretly cut off the skirt of his cloak and took it. And when the king had gone out, David came forward and called out after Saul. And the king turned at the voice. And David did obeisance and said, "Do not believe slanders. Behold, the Lord delivered you into my hands; for when in the cave I cut off the skirt of your cloak, it was easy for me to kill you also." And at the same time he showed him the piece, and cried out, "May the Lord judge between me and you." And Saul, pierced to the heart at this, lifted up his voice and, weeping, said to David, "You are righteous; for I have been the cause of evils to you, but you have repaid me with good. Whence I am persuaded that God is keeping you to be king of Israel. Give me, then, pledges that you will not destroy my house, but will preserve my line." And David swore to Saul, and they departed from one another.

32. At that time too Samuel the prophet died, a righteous and good man, who had ruled Israel after Eli, alone for twelve years, but together with Saul for eighteen. And David went into the wilderness of Maon. And he sent to Nabal the Carmelite, a rich man who was shearing his flocks, those who should greet him and ask him to give to those with him and to himself, as he might choose, since they had kept his flocks and his shepherds untouched. But Nabal, being harsh and insolent, answered David's men inhumanly and shamelessly, saying, "Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse?" and calling him a runaway. At this David is angered, and swore to destroy all that belonged to Nabal, and set out against him with four hundred armed men. But Nabal's wife, being sensible and fair, having learned both how David had greeted her husband and how he had kept their property unharmed, and what blasphemous things Nabal had answered David, without communicating anything to her own husband, taking on donkeys gifts of every kind and many, set out to David. And meeting him, she did obeisance, and begged him not to bear a grudge against her husband; for his disposition was according to his name—for Nabal means "folly"—but to lay aside his anger and to receive what was offered. And he both praised the woman and, granting pardon, returned. And the woman, returning to Nabal, made known to him David's coming. And he, seized by fear and grief, surviving not more than ten days, broke off his life. And learning this, David sent to Abigail, wooing her for himself. And she said she was not worthy to dwell with such a man; nevertheless she went, and David took her as his wife.
But Saul still plotted against him, and with three thousand chosen men encamps by the hill of Hachilah, where David was passing his time with the six hundred men who were with him. And by night David himself and Amesa went into the camp of Saul, and they entered where Saul was sleeping. And when Amesa set out to kill him, David did not allow it, but, taking the king's spear and the vessel of water, they went out without anyone perceiving, and this though Abner, the commander of his army, and many others lay around the king. And going up to the top of the mountain, David called out to Abner, "Why is it that you do not guard the king? For behold, some men came in to kill him, and you have not known it. Look, then, for the spear and the flask of water, and you will know what a danger has passed you by." And Saul, recognizing David's voice, and how he had spared him again when able to kill him, said that he had sinned and acted foolishly, and exhorted him to take courage and to return to his house. And he said, "May the Lord render to each according to his righteousness and his faith." And David went away with the six hundred who were with him to Achish the king of Gath, and passed four months there. And when the Palestinians wished to make war against Israel, Achish said to David, "Will you go out with me to the war, you and those with you?" And he readily promised to be his ally. But when the foreigners had now advanced into the country of the Israelites, Saul was thrown into confusion and inquired of God whether he should fight. And when He did not answer, he sought out a woman with a familiar spirit and went to her in disguise, that it might not be recognized who he was, and asked that the soul of Samuel be brought up for him. And when, by certain incantations, Saul supposed it had been brought up, he said, "I am greatly distressed, because the foreigners have gathered against me and the Lord has departed from me." And the phantom of Samuel answered, "The Lord has done to you what he foretold through me, and he takes away your kingdom and gives it to David, and subjects the people to the enemy; and you and your sons shall fall tomorrow." And Saul, greatly grieved at hearing this, departed. And the foreigners encamped, and David and the six hundred with him were behind. But it did not please the satraps that David should march with them, saying, "Lest he do us some harm by joining his own people in the battle," and they asked that he be sent back. And Achish, persuaded by the satraps, commanded David to depart. And he went away with those who were with him, and found Ziklag, which Achish had given him for a dwelling, burned with fire, and his two wives and all who were there taken captive by the Amalekites. And David and those with him lamented over this, and he asked God through the high priest Abiathar whether he should pursue after them. And when God permitted it, he pursued with the four hundred, leaving the two hundred to guard the baggage. And finding them scattered, eating and drinking, and falling upon them suddenly, he killed them all except four hundred who had fled on swift camels, and recovered all the spoil. But the four hundred with David, returning, were unwilling that the two hundred too should share with them, and demanded to be content with the recovery of their own wives. But David judged this opinion unjust, and declared that the gain should be divided equally among all. And from that time this became a law also, commanding that those who guarded the baggage should share equally in the spoils with those who fought. And when a battle broke out between the Israelites and the Palestinians, very many of the Hebrews are killed, and the three sons of Saul fell, and Saul himself was wounded in the lower abdomen. And knowing that he had been struck mortally and would not live, he told his armor-bearer to run him through, that he might not be taken alive by the enemy. And when he would not do what was commanded, Saul himself fell upon his sword and died. And his armor-bearer, when he saw the king fallen, killed himself also. And on the next day, while the foreigners were stripping the fallen of the Israelites, they came upon the bodies of Saul and his sons on the mountains of Gilboa, and cutting off their heads, they sent them into their own country, making a show of them everywhere and announcing the good news, and they dedicated their armor to their own gods, but crucified the bodies by the wall of Methsam, which was afterward called Scythopolis. But when the inhabitants of the city of Jabesh in Gilead learned what had befallen Saul, the strongest of them went out, and pressing their march through the whole night, they took down the bodies of Saul and Jonathan, and carrying them to Jabesh, they burned them, and gathering the bones, they buried them. And Saul reigned eighteen years while Samuel was still living, and after his death twenty-two.

1. Nebuzaradan, having razed Jerusalem, conveyed to Babylon the people and the high priest Saraeas and the sacred vessels. Nabuchodonosor dedicated the vessels of God to his own gods, and settled the captives in his own country. Those who during the siege had deserted to the Babylonians, and the poor, Nebuzaradan left behind in Judaea, and set over them as governor Godolias, a man of good family, fair and just, and charged them to work the land and ordered them to pay tribute to Nabuchodonosor. The prophet Jeremiah he urged to go off to Babylon; but he wished to remain among the ruins of his homeland. And he left him there, charging Godolias to take all care of him. He released to him also his disciple Baruch, who was exceptionally learned in the ancestral tongue. As many as had fled from Jerusalem on account of the siege came to Godolias. And he counselled them to farm the land and to dwell in whatever city each one wished, and to rebuild the ruins. Recognizing Godolias to be a worthy man, they loved him greatly.

There returned with the others also one named Ishmael, who was of the royal line, who had fled to the Ammonites at the time of the siege. When he came to Godolias, certain men said that he was plotting against him; and if he would allow them to kill the man, he would escape the plot. But Godolias would not believe it, and said he counted it better to die himself than to kill a man who had trusted himself to him. After a time this Ishmael came with others to Godolias, and being entertained as a guest he killed both Godolias and those feasting with him. Then, falling upon by night the Babylonians left in the city, he killed both them and all the Jews there. On the next day, when eighty men from the country came to Godolias with gifts, Ishmael killed these too, save a few who promised to show him household goods and clothing and grain hidden in the fields. And taking many captives with him, he went off to the Ammonites. Learning this, certain leaders of the Jews, having spurred on those with them, pursued him; and they recovered the captives, but Ishmael with eight men escaped.

The survivors, fearing the Babylonians, deliberated about going off to Egypt. Though Jeremiah counselled them to remain—for if they remained, the deity would provide that they suffer no harm, but if they departed, would not be with them—they did not believe him, but disobeying they set out for Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch with them. When the prophet had gone there, the deity revealed to him what was to come. And he foretold to his countrymen that the Babylonian would march against the Egyptians and master Egypt, and that he would kill some of them and lead the rest off as spear-won captives. For this he was stoned by his fellow-countrymen and died. But the things he had foretold came to pass; for the fifth year after the sack of Jerusalem was being completed when Nabuchodonosor set out against Coele-Syria, and having taken it he came against the Ammonites and Moabites, and from there marched against Egypt, and subduing it killed the king and set up another in his place, and removed the Jews there to Babylon. When Jeremiah had been buried in Egypt, it is said that king Alexander, having become master of Egypt, since the Egyptians sang the prophet's praises, removed his bones, along with other things, to the city founded by him, Alexandria.

The prophet, then, foretold, as I have said, the things that were to come; and the race of the Hebrews found such an end, removed beyond the Euphrates. For the ten tribes, while Hoshea reigned in Samaria, were taken captive by the Assyrians, and the two tribes afterward were taken spear-won by Nabuchodonosor, and all who were left after the capture of Jerusalem. And Shalmaneser removed the nation of the Cuthaeans from Persia to Samaria, while Nabuchodonosor left Judaea desolate, and it remained thus for seventy years. The time between the captivity of the ten tribes from Samaria and that of the two from Jerusalem came to a hundred and thirty years, six months, and ten days.

2. The Babylonian made eunuchs of the more nobly born of the captive children, both those related to king Zedekiah and the more vigorous and comely of the rest, and handing them over to tutors he had them taught both the letters of the Chaldaeans and the native lore, assigning them their diet from his own table. Four of the children were of the royal stock, fair in appearance and good in their natures; of whom the Babylonian renamed the one called Daniel Baltasar, the one named Ananias he called Shadrach, the other called Mishael Meshach, and the remaining one, Azarias, Abednego. These he held in greater honour than the rest, since through their natural gifts they advanced in wisdom. These youths, then, begged the eunuch who had charge of them not to feed them on what was provided from the royal table, but on pulse and dates and other such things. He said he feared that, fed on such fare, their bodies might grow thin, and that on this account he himself might be ill-treated by the king. But they begged him to feed them thus for ten days, and if their bodily condition was not changed, to feed them so for the future too, but if he saw their bodies wasting, to keep to the former diet. The one in charge of the children was persuaded by this, and having done so, when he saw that they suffered nothing from such food—but rather had become more flourishing than the rest—he gave them lifeless foods. And they, with their minds made keen, mastered all Chaldaean and Assyrian learning. And Daniel devoted his zeal also to the interpretation of dreams.

Then Nabuchodonosor, having beheld an extraordinary dream, and having learned its interpretation in his sleep, forgot both the dream and its interpretation. At dawn, therefore, summoning the Chaldaeans and the seers and magi, he demanded of them that they tell him both the dream and its meaning. But they wished him first to tell the dream, and so to ask from them its significance. The king was angered at this and condemned them all to death, when they said they could not discover the dream. With these, as being wise men, Daniel and the three children were both summoned and condemned. Daniel therefore went to the commander of the king's bodyguard, and asked that the execution of those condemned be put off for one night; "for perhaps," he said, "during it we shall beg of God and learn the dream." The king yielded to the request. And Daniel, taking with him his three kinsmen children, supplicated God through the night. There was therefore revealed to him from God both the dream and what it signified. And after a day he went off to the king and said that both the dream and its interpretation had been made known to him from God, who had pitied those in danger of dying unjustly for it; "and no less you too, who wished without cause to kill so many for demanding what is impossible, things knowable to the divine nature alone. What you saw is this. You seemed to see a great statue standing, whose head was of gold, but whose shoulders and arms were of silver, while the belly with the thighs was of bronze, and the shins and the feet were partly of iron and partly of clay. Then a stone, broken off from a mountain, seemed to fall upon the statue and shatter it, and to grind the gold and the silver and the bronze and the iron and the clay so fine that they were winnowed away by the wind and scattered. And the stone seemed to grow and to come to so great a size that the whole earth was filled by it. This, then, is your dream; and what is revealed to you by it, as you take thought concerning the kingdom and who will rule after you, is this. The golden head is both you and the remaining kings of the Babylonians, and the gold indicates the great prosperity of your rule; the two hands and the shoulders represent two kingdoms by which your dominion will be destroyed; the bronze belly and the like thighs indicate a king clad in bronze, who will overthrow those who destroyed you; and his kingdom in turn another, more powerful, will bring to an end; for iron is stronger than gold and silver and bronze." For gold, and especially the purest, is softer than silver; and silver is denser than gold, but softer than bronze; and iron again is firmer than bronze. The kingdom of the Assyrians, then, is likened to the head, as being earlier than the others and leading in time. The second he called the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, who destroyed the rule of the Assyrians. For Cyrus, as will be related, was a Persian on his father's side, but related to the Medes through his mother; he, taking both nations together and making war on the Assyrians, overthrew their kingdom. By the pair of the hands the pair of these two nations is represented. The third kingdom he calls that of the Macedonians. This he likened to bronze as being stronger, inasmuch as it overthrew the Persian rule. And by the belly the monarchy of Alexander is figured, and by the thighs the division of the kingdom after his death and its parceling out. The fourth kingdom he called that of the Romans, to which he assigned iron because of its hardness. He figured it by the shins because it was later in time; for the kingdom of the Romans was later than the other great kingdoms, and the shins and the feet are the last parts of the body. The clay mixed with the iron hints that the kingdom is strong, but has in itself something brittle and weak; for such is the nature of clay, composed of mud.

3. If one were minded to refer the vision to the earlier constitution of the Roman dominion, when the senate and the dictators and the consuls and the tribunes and the people held the management of public affairs, he will find in many places the people at variance with the senate and factions arising, the senate enacting some things and the multitude introducing others, so that from this they fought one another and their affairs through this discord sometimes inclined to the worse and weaker. One might figure the senate by iron, on account of the firmness of its judgement, but the multitude might be likened to clay, being mingled with the magistrates and the council, both because of its rabble-like and grovelling quality—for such is the mud from which clay is made—and because of the fickleness and weakness of its disposition. For the multitude is wont to be unstable and easily led and easily changed of mind; and one will find these things often happened to the Roman state, going through the ancient writings about it.

If, then, one were to refer the difference of the materials and their mixture to the earlier constitution of the Roman state, he would perhaps reckon thus; but if to the later, when affairs were brought by the Romans from aristocracy to monarchy, and to the subsequent establishment of the empire, then too he would find that the discord of the Romans with one another brought the greatest harm to the state. For Caesar, reaching after monarchy, set on foot civil wars against Magnus Pompey and the others who claimed the ancient liberty; and against those who had killed him, in turn, Caesar Augustus and Antony got up the like battles; then again these two, at variance with one another over sole rule, set in motion grievous wars, kindred being destroyed on both sides in all the battles, and from this the Roman power being diminished. Nor would one see the factions abating in later times either. And if one compares the nature of the iron and the clay with the later empire, he will find the Roman rule in one respect strong, in another weak, and having cast away the most of its old dominion, and now circumscribed within a small fraction of that ancient sway.

Such, then, are the matters of the four kingdoms. But the remaining and indestructible kingdom, which the stone figured—the stone that was cut without hands and ground fine the materials of which the image was composed, and filled the whole earth, which the prophet said would not be destroyed unto the ages—this would be the future manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ, which will appear when the iron kingdom has become weaker through the admixture of the clay; when all things will be subjected to him, and he will deem worthy of an unending and incorruptible kingdom those who have made themselves worthy of it. For Scripture is wont to call Christ a stone. For David said, "The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner," and Isaiah, in the person of God, says, "Behold, I lay in Zion a cornerstone." And the great Paul calls Christ a cornerstone, upon whom he wrote that believers are built. And again he says, "No one can lay another foundation than the one laid, which is Jesus Christ." And again elsewhere, "They drank of a spiritual following rock, and the rock was Christ." And he is called a rock of offence and a stone of stumbling, and in many places the Lord would be found called stone and rock. The being cut without hands prefigured his birth above nature, without seed, apart from marital union. For the tribe of Judah, from which David sprang, may be reckoned the mountain; and Christ is the stone, cut from it in respect of his humanity; and without hands, because he came forth not according to the natural laws, but from an unwedded and holy womb.
