To the captive men he said, "Go, work your land and dwell in your houses and live with your wives and enjoy your children, and announce these things to the rest; for there will be one new thing for you, that the same man will not rule you as before, but in all else things will be the same for you." So they, doing obeisance, departed; and Cyrus said, "It is now time, Medes and Armenians, to dine; suppers are prepared for you as we, my good men, were able. And do you too, Hyrcanians," he said, "lead them to the tents, the rulers to the greatest, the rest as seems best, and dine yourselves too; for the tents are whole and untouched for you." And they did as ordered. And Cyrus sent many of the Persians around to watch the camp, that if anyone approached from outside, he might not escape notice, and if any of those within tried to slip away, he might be caught. So the Persians passed the time. On the next day he ordered the spoils to be distributed to the soldiers, and the horses to be given to the Persians, that they too might be horsemen. "And for Cyaxares," he said, "choose such things as you know to be pleasing to him; and for the Persians," he said, "those with me, whatever is left over will suffice; for we have not been reared in luxury, so that perhaps you would laugh at us if you put something stately about us; as I know we shall give you much to laugh at, both seated on the horses and, I think, falling to the ground." And calling the captains, he ordered them to take the horses, and to take them by lot, each an equal number.

19. Meanwhile there came Gobryas, an aged Assyrian man, with a mounted retinue, and asked to see Cyrus. He was brought to him and said, "Master, I am by race an Assyrian, having also a strong fortress, and I rule much land; I have also horse to a thousand, which I used to provide to the king of the Assyrians, and I was his friend as much as possible. But since he is dead at your hands, and his son holds the rule, who is most hostile to me because he envied and killed my only and beloved son, I have come to you and give myself to you as servant and ally, and ask you to become my avenger." And Cyrus answered, "If, Gobryas, all that you say is also what you mean, I receive you as suppliant and promise, with the gods, to avenge for you the murder of your son." And he said, "On these terms, speaking truly, I give you my right hand and take yours."

When this was done, he bade Gobryas depart, keeping his arms too. And he departed. And the Medes were present, having chosen for Cyrus the fairest tent and the Susian woman, who is said to have been the fairest woman in Asia, and two of the best music-girls, and for Cyaxares the second choice; and the remaining tents they handed over to Cyrus for the Persians. But Cyrus ordered Cyaxares' goods to be kept by his nearest people, and said, "What is given to me I gladly receive." And calling Araspes the Mede, who had been his companion from boyhood, he ordered him to guard for him the woman and the tent. She was the wife of Abradates the king of Susa, who, when the camp was taken, was not present, having been sent about an alliance by the Assyrian to the king of the Bactrians, being his guest-friend.

Rising at dawn they went off to Gobryas, Cyrus on horseback and the horsemen of the Persians now amounting to two thousand. On the second day, about evening, they came to Gobryas's place, they and the allies. Learning there that the Assyrians at Babylon had prepared a force many times the former one, he said, "Lead us straight on toward Babylon." As they journeyed, on the fourth day they came to the borders of Gobryas's land, and were now in the enemy's country, and he kept with him the foot and some of the horse, and let the other horsemen ride about, ordering them to kill those they met who had arms, and to bring to him the rest and whatever booty they took. He bade the Persians too ride about with them. And many of them came back tumbled from their horses, and many bringing as much booty as possible. Then he went toward Babylon as if drawn up for battle. When the Assyrians did not come out against him, Cyrus ordered Gobryas to ride up and say, if the king wished to come out and fight for his land, that he too would fight with him; but if he would not defend the land, that it was necessary to obey the victors. So Gobryas rode up and said this; and the Assyrian sent and said, "Your master, Gobryas, answers: If you wish to fight, come on the thirtieth day; for now we are not yet at leisure; we are still preparing."

And he reported this to Cyrus, who led the army back, and asked Gobryas about Gadatas. Now Gadatas was the son of a certain king, a companion of the Assyrian, whom, while drinking with him, he seized and gelded and made a eunuch; who, when his father died, then held the kingdom, being a eunuch. To this man, then, Cyrus wished Gobryas to go and bring him to himself. And he went. And meeting him and saying all that Cyrus charged, he returned, and Gadatas, pretending to ally with the Assyrian and by guile seizing a certain fortress of the Assyrian, an outwork of the war, and handing it over to Cyrus, came himself too to Cyrus. And being received he heard, "Gadatas, the Assyrian, it seems, deprived you of getting children, but did not deprive you of acquiring friends." So he spoke. The fortress having come under Cyrus, both Cadusians and Sacae and Hyrcanians in greater numbers joined his army; and upon this Gadatas comes to Cyrus saying that the Assyrian, learning about the fortress and being enraged, was making ready to invade my land. "If, then, you let me go, I would try to save the walls; for the rest I have less concern." Cyrus asked, "If you go, when will you be home?" And he said, "On the third day I will dine in our land." "And I," said Cyrus, "on what day might I arrive there with the army?" And Gadatas answered, "You could not, master, unless you came in six or seven days." And Cyrus said, "Do you, then, go off most quickly, and I will go as I am able." And Gadatas departed, and Cyrus said to the commanders of the allies that they must help Gadatas, who was being warred on by the Assyrian, a benefactor. And all agreed. And he said, "Since it seems good to you too, come, let us go, taking the strongest of horse and men and three days' provisions, that we may go light." And having so equipped themselves, at midnight they took to the road, Gobryas leading them.

20. So Cyrus departed; but as Gadatas was going off, one of his own powerful men plotted against him, and sending to the Assyrian disclosed the force of Gadatas and that he was coming, and charged him to lie in ambush for him, that he might so take both Gadatas himself and those with him. When the Assyrian heard this, he laid an ambush. And as Gadatas came near the ambush and now seemed to be at the point of being taken, the ambush rose up. And the one plotting against Gadatas at this moment struck him, and hit him on the shoulder, not mortally however; and having done this he at once withdrew to the Assyrian and pursued with him. So some of Gadatas's men were taken, and some fled, turning their reins; and now they descry Cyrus approaching. When he understood the matter, he led his army against them. And the enemy, seeing this, turned to flight, and Cyrus ordered the pursuit. And men and chariots were taken, and many were slain, including the very man who had struck Gadatas; and the rest and the Assyrian himself fled to a certain great city of his. And Cyrus, having accomplished this, withdrew to Gadatas's land, and went to visit Gadatas. And Gadatas met him with his wound bound up, and acknowledged his gratitude, saying, "As far as concerned me, I am lost, but as far as concerns you, I am saved, since you helped me so readily."

The Cadusians, posted then as rearguard by Cyrus and having had no share in the pursuit, wishing to do some brilliant thing themselves, without communicating with Cyrus, overran Babylonia. The Assyrian, going out of the city to which he had fled, fell in with them; and learning they were alone, he attacked them, and killed both their ruler and many others, and pursuing for some distance turned back. Those of the Cadusians who were saved came toward evening to the camp. Cyrus handed the wounded over to those who would heal them, and to the rest he himself addressed words of encouragement, and counselled them to choose a ruler for themselves from among themselves. And they chose one. And Gadatas came bringing Cyrus gifts of all kinds and many, and very many horses. But Cyrus said he received the horses, that he might fill out the Persian cavalry and that his horsemen might come to ten thousand, but ordered the money to be taken back to him and kept until he should see Cyrus too able to give in return; and he counselled him to put his city under safe guard, and himself to march with him. And Gadatas was pleased with the counsel, and having equipped himself accompanied Cyrus. As he journeyed thus and came to the border between the Syrians and Medes, there being three fortresses of the Syrians there, the one he himself took by assault and force, while the other two Cyrus, by frightening, and Gadatas, by persuading, brought the guards to surrender.

Then he sent to Cyaxares, asking him to come to the camp, that they might deliberate about what they needed. And the messenger went off; and Cyrus ordered the tent which the Medes had chosen for Cyaxares to be furnished as well as possible, both with the other equipment and by bringing the woman into the women's quarters of the tent, and with her the music-girls who had been chosen for Cyaxares. Meanwhile the messenger reported Cyrus's words to Cyaxares, and he set out with the Median horsemen who had stayed with him. When Cyrus knew he was approaching, taking the horsemen of the Persians, now many, and the Medes present and the Armenians and the best-mounted of the other allies, he went to meet him, displaying his force to Cyaxares. But Cyaxares, seeing Cyrus followed by many good men, and himself by a small and worthless retinue, thought it a dishonour to him, and grief took him, and he was reduced to open tears. Cyrus, taking him aside privately and seating him beside him, conversed with him, and asked the cause of his anger and grief. And having said and heard much, at last he said, "By the gods, uncle, cease for now blaming me; and when you have made trial of us, how we stand toward you, then either acknowledge gratitude to me or blame me." And Cyaxares yielded; and Cyrus, coming up, kissed him. And when the Medes and the Persians and the rest saw this, they were overjoyed. Mounting their horses, then, Cyrus and Cyaxares went off to the camp, and led Cyaxares to the tent chosen for him. And the Medes came to him bringing gifts, each one of the fairest thing he had taken. And when it was time for supper, Cyaxares was about his supper, while Cyrus took thought how the allies might stay with him, and gathering enough of his friends to help him do what was needful, he asked them to contrive how they might persuade the allies not to leave them, but to help still. On the next day all gathered to Cyaxares; and before they met him the friends brought to Cyrus, one this, another that, of the allied nations, who begged him to remain and share in the war with him.

21. Meanwhile Cyaxares, coming out of the tent, said, "Fellow-allies, it is necessary to consider whether it seems a time still to make war or now to disband the army." Each, then, coming forward, spoke, and all gave the judgement that they must make war. After all, Cyrus said, "Nor does it escape me, men, that if we disband the army, our affairs would become weaker, while those of the enemy would grow. But I see opponents approaching whom we shall not be able to fight. For winter is coming on and a lack of provisions. For some have been used up by us, and some, because of us, have been carried off by the enemy into strongholds. Who, then, fighting with hunger and cold, could make war? I think we ought to take away the enemy's strongholds, and make for ourselves as many strongholds as possible. For if we have fortresses, these will estrange the country from the enemy, and be to our profit." When these and many such things were said, all said they would zealously join in these, and Cyaxares himself, and they resolved to make siege-engines. But Cyrus, knowing there would be a delay about these things, both put the army in safety, and led it out on foraging expeditions, that they might have provisions in abundance and might be the healthier for their toil, and that they might be reminded of good discipline.

Deserters coming from Babylon said that the Assyrian had gone off to Lydia bringing many talents of gold and silver and all manner of adornment. The mass of the soldiers said he was now removing his money in fear; but Cyrus said the Assyrian was going off to seek allies, and made counter-preparations as though a battle would still be needed. It seemed good to him also to send a scout to Lydia, that he might learn what the Assyrian was doing. And for this Araspes seemed suitable to him—the one guarding the fair woman—who, smitten with love of the woman, had made advances to her; but she refused and was faithful to her husband even in his absence, and indeed reported Araspes to Cyrus. When the lover threatened her that, if she would not yield willingly, he would do it unwillingly, she, fearing the violence, sent the eunuch to Cyrus and bade him tell all. And he, hearing it, laughed, and sent Artabazus with the eunuch, ordering him to tell Araspes not to force such a woman, but to persuade her if he could; he said he did not forbid that. And Araspes, hearing this, was plunged into grief, partly from shame, partly from fear. Cyrus, knowing this, called him aside and said, "Cease, Araspes, being afraid and ashamed. For I hear that the gods too are overcome by love, and I know that men, and very prudent ones, have suffered things from love. And I am the cause of this to you, who shut you up with such an irresistible thing." And Araspes answered, "But you, Cyrus, are gentle in this too and forgiving of human faults; but other men plunge me into grief. For my enemies rejoice over me, and my friends counsel me to get out of the way, lest I suffer something from you." And Cyrus said, "Know well, then, that by this opinion you can both do me a favour and benefit the allies." "Would," said Araspes, "that I might be useful to you at a crisis." "If, then," he said, "pretending to flee from me, you should go over to the enemy, you would be trusted by them." "Yes, by Zeus," said Araspes, "and by my friends too." "You would go, then," he said, "reporting to us all the enemy's affairs."

Araspes, then, so going forth and taking his most faithful servants, departed. And Panthea, learning this, sent to Cyrus and said, "Do not grieve, Cyrus, that Araspes has gone over to the enemy; for if you let me send to my husband, there will come to you a friend more faithful than Araspes." And Cyrus bade her send; and she sent. And Abradates, when he knew the tokens from his wife, gladly went over to Cyrus. When he was at the outposts he sent to Cyrus saying who he was. And Cyrus ordered him to be brought to the woman. When the woman and Abradates saw one another, they embraced from a state of despair. Then Panthea told of the holiness and temperance of Cyrus and his compassion toward her. Upon this Abradates comes to Cyrus, and taking hold of his right hand said, "In return for the good you have done us, Cyrus, I give myself to you as friend and servant and ally." And Cyrus said, "And I receive you."

22. Money came to Cyrus from the Indian, and those bringing it reported that the Indian said, "I am glad, Cyrus, that you made known to me concerning your needs, and I wish to be your guest-friend, and I send you money, and if you need more, send for it; and my men are charged to do whatever you bid." And Cyrus said, "I bid, then, that the rest remain where you have encamped and guard the money, but that three of you come to me into the enemy as though from the Indian about an alliance, and learning the things there, whatever they say and do, report to me and to the Indian as quickly as possible." So the Indians, having equipped themselves, set out the next day, and Cyrus prepared his war-affairs magnificently. For the Persian horsemen were now full to ten thousand, and there were scythe-bearing chariots to a hundred, and Abradates fashioned another hundred, and the Median chariots they put together, another hundred, remade in the same fashion from the Trojan and Libyan driving; and on the camels were posted two archers on each. As Cyrus's war-affairs were being so ordered, the Indians came from the enemy and said that Croesus had been chosen leader and general, and that many kings and many nations and Greeks were ready to ally. When Cyrus's army heard this, they fell into anxiety. When Cyrus perceived fear running through the army, he conversed with them and turned them to a more cheerful temper. Then he said, "It seems to me, men, that we should go against them as quickly as possible." And all agreed. Cyaxares, then, with a third part of the Medes remained behind, that the home country too might not be left desolate, but Cyrus went on as quickly as he could. When the advance scouts seemed to make out smoke or dust rising, and to see men taking fodder and wood, they guessed the enemy's army was somewhere near, and reported to Cyrus. He ordered them to remain at the lookouts and report whatever they saw, and sent a squadron of horse forward to take some prisoners. They, dashing down into the plain, seized men and brought them. And the captives said they were from the camp. And Cyrus said, "How far off from here is the army?" And they said, two parasangs. And he asked further, "Was there any talk of us among them?" "Yes, by Zeus," they said, "and much, that you were now near, approaching." "What then?" said Cyrus, "did they rejoice to hear we were coming?" "No, by Zeus," they said, "but were greatly grieved." "And who is it that marshals them?" said Cyrus. And they answered, "Croesus himself, and a certain Greek man, and a certain Mede, who was said to be a fugitive from you." And Cyrus to this, "O Zeus, may it be mine to take him as I wish." He ordered the captives to be led away. There was not much interval, and the scout sent long ago, Araspes, that is, is announced to be riding up. When Cyrus heard, leaping up he went to meet him and greeted him, while the others were astounded at the matter, until Cyrus said, "Friends, there has come to us a most excellent man, who went off not overcome by anything shameful, fearing me, but sent by me, that learning the enemy's affairs clearly he might report to us. All must therefore honour this man. For he both underwent dishonour and ran into danger for our good." From then all greeted Araspes. And Cyrus said, "Relate, Araspes, all that you have seen." And he related the number of the enemy and the place of their array and the plans of the enemy. And Cyrus ordered each to go off and inspect his own arms and horses, and at dawn to make ready for battle.

Then, then, they departed; and on the next day each armed himself, and Abradates, having drawn by lot to be posted opposite the Egyptians. As he was arming, Panthea brought a golden helmet and arm-pieces and bracelets about the wrists of his hands and a purple tunic reaching to the feet and a crest dyed hyacinth-blue, which she herself had made for her husband. And he, seeing them, said, "You surely, wife, having broken up your own adornment, made the arms for me?" "Yes, by Zeus," said Panthea, "for you are to me the greatest adornment." And saying this she put the arms on her husband, and tried to weep unseen, but the tears fell down her cheeks. When Abradates was now ready to mount the chariot, Panthea, bidding those present withdraw, said, "That I honour you, Abradates, even above my own life, I think you know; nevertheless, being so disposed toward you, I swear by my love and yours that I would rather, with you having proved a good man, be buried in common with you than live in shame with one who is shamed. And to Cyrus I think we owe great gratitude, that when I was made captive and chosen for him he treated me neither as a slave nor as a free woman in a dishonourable name, but kept me for you as one taking a brother's wife. Moreover, when Araspes who guarded me deserted from him, I promised him that, if he would let me send to you so that you should come, you would prove far more faithful and better than Araspes." So she spoke, and Abradates, marveling at her words, prayed, "Grant, O Zeus, that I appear a man worthy of Panthea and a friend worthy of Cyrus." Saying this he mounted the chariot.

23. Cyrus, gathering the leaders, harangued them, encouraging them to the battle, and so set out to go. When they drew near the opposing forces, so as to see one another, Cyrus marshaled his men as well as possible, and going along the ranks he sharpened the men for battle with words. And Croesus, setting his own army opposite Cyrus's force, signaled to them to advance against the enemy. And three phalanxes came on, one in front, and of the two, one on the right, the other on the left, so that fear came upon all Cyrus's army; for it was surrounded by the enemy on every side except behind. Nevertheless Cyrus's men too, when he gave the order, all turned to face the enemy. And there was for a while much silence on every side; and when it seemed to Cyrus to be the time, he began a paean, and the whole army shouted it with him. And Cyrus rose up and with the horsemen engaged the enemy, while the foot drawn up with him followed. And Artagerses, commander of those on the camels, attacked on the left, sending the camels forward, as Cyrus had ordered. And the horses from afar would not endure them, but some fled, some leaped aside, some fell on one another. And the chariots, on the right and the left, charged at once, and many fleeing these were caught by them. And Abradates, crying "Friends, follow," drove on, sparing none of his horses; and the other charioteers charged with him. And Abradates broke into the phalanx of the Egyptians, and with him broke in those nearest posted, while the others swerved aside after the fleeing chariots. And those about Abradates, striking with the rush of the horses, overturned some and ran over those who fell; and whatever the scythes caught, all was forcibly cut through, both arms and bodies. In this indescribable confusion, the wheels leaping over the heaps of all sorts, Abradates falls out, and others too of those who had charged with him. And these were cut to pieces, while the Persians, following close, killed the disordered Egyptians, but those who held together advanced against the Persians; and there was a fierce battle. The Egyptians had the advantage both in number and in arms. The Persians could not hold out, but drew back step by step, striking and being struck, until they came under the engines. When they came there, the Egyptians were struck again from the towers. There was much slaughter of men, much din of arms, much shouting. Meanwhile Cyrus, pursuing those opposite him, comes up. And seeing the Persians forced from their ground, he was grieved, and ordering those with him to follow, rode round to the rear; and falling on them they killed many. When the Egyptians perceived it, they turned about. And foot and horse fought in confusion; and a man fallen under Cyrus's horse and being trodden struck his horse in the belly with a sword, and the horse, convulsing from the blow, shakes Cyrus off. And at once all cried out and falling on fought. And one of Cyrus's attendants, leaping down, set him on his own horse. And when he had mounted, he saw the Egyptians now being struck on every side. And going along by the engines he went up onto one of the towers, and looked down upon the plain full of horses, men, chariots, fleeing, pursuing, mastering, being mastered, but nowhere could he see anything still standing except that of the Egyptians. These, surrounded on every side, sat under their shields, doing nothing now, but suffering many and dreadful things. And Cyrus, admiring them and pitying them, that good men were perishing, allowed no one to fight with them any more, but sent heralds to them asking whether they wished all to perish or to be saved. And they said, "By doing what fair thing might we be saved?" And Cyrus said, "If you give up your arms to us, who choose to save you, though we might destroy you." Hearing this, the Egyptians gave pledges and received them.

Having accomplished this, Cyrus, now in the dark, withdrew and encamped. And those about Cyrus, having supped, slept; but Croesus at once fled to Sardis with his army, and the other nations withdrew in the night where they could. At dawn Cyrus led on toward Sardis, and coming to the city set up his engines and prepared ladders. On the following night he sent up Chaldaeans and Persians by what seemed the steepest part of the Sardian fortress. A Persian man, a slave of one of the guards on the citadel, led the way for these. When the heights were taken, the Lydians fled from the walls. Cyrus at daybreak entered the city, charging that no one from the ranks should move. Croesus, shut up in the palace, called for Cyrus. And Cyrus left guards over Croesus, and having encamped his men went off to Croesus. And seeing him Croesus said, "Hail, master." "And you too," said Cyrus, "Croesus. But would you be willing to give me some counsel?" "I would be willing," he said, "Cyrus." "I, then, Croesus," he said, "seeing the soldiers worn out and having run very many risks and now thinking they hold the richest city in Asia after Babylon, I judge it right that the soldiers be benefited, but I do not wish to let them plunder the city." And Croesus said, "But let me speak to those of the Lydians whom I wish, that I have brought it about with you that there be no pillage; and know that there will be for you, from willing Lydians, everything precious in Sardis. But first send to my treasures and take what you wish."

Cyrus agreed to do this, and they passed the day on these matters; on the next, Cyrus, calling some of his friends, ordered some to take the treasures, and others to take whatever money Croesus delivered. Then he asked whether anyone had seen Abradates; and when one of the attendants said that he had died in the battle, he struck his thigh, and leaping on his horse rode to him. And when he saw Panthea sitting on the ground and the corpse lying, he wept and said, "Alas, good and faithful soul." And the woman said, "I know that it was for my sake that he suffered this, and perhaps, Cyrus, for yours too. For I, fool that I was, often urged him to appear a friend worthy of mention to you, and he himself considered how he might do you a favour. And he has died blamelessly, while I, who urged him, sit beside him alive." And Cyrus for some time wept in silence, then spoke many consolations for the grief, and went off. And the woman bade the eunuchs withdraw, but told her nurse to remain and, when she was dead, to cover both her and her husband with one garment. The nurse sat weeping; but she slew herself, and laying her own head upon her husband's breast she died. And the nurse wailed and covered them both. And the eunuchs, learning what had happened, being three, drawing their scimitars, slew themselves. And Cyrus, when he perceived the woman's deed, admired her and mourned her, and heaped over them a vast monument, burying them magnificently.

24. The Carians, having fallen into faction and warring with one another, both parties surrendered themselves to Cyrus; and those of Phrygia by the Hellespont gave very many gifts to Cyrus, so as not to receive barbarians into their walls, but to pay tribute to him and to march wherever Cyrus bade. But the king of the Phrygians prepared as if not about to make peace; and when his subordinates revolted from him, he came to grips with Hystaspes. And Hystaspes, leaving Persian garrisons in the heights, went off, bringing with his own men many Phrygian horsemen and peltasts. And Cyrus set out from Sardis, leaving a garrison in Sardis, having Croesus with him bringing very many wagons full of much and varied money, and having accurately written down how much was in each wagon. And he gave the writings to Cyrus; and Cyrus said, "You have done well, Croesus; but those who have taken the money will surely bring it all to me, and if they steal anything, they will steal their own." And Croesus brought also many Lydians, splendidly armed.

Going on toward Babylon, Cyrus subdued the Phrygians in Greater Phrygia, and subdued the Cappadocians, and made subjects of the Arabians; and from all these he equipped of the Persians horsemen not fewer than forty thousand, and to all the allies he distributed many of the captured horses. He came, then, to Babylon bringing many horsemen, and many archers and javelin-men, and slingers innumerable. When he was at Babylon, he set the army about it, and himself, going round with the commanders of the allies and his friends, surveyed the walls. Then he brought the army up and encamped about the city. And seeing the river there flowing into the city and passing through the middle of Babylon, he disclosed his plan to no one, but ordered a trench to be dug around the camp, broad and very deep, that they might perhaps need the fewest guards in the camp. Those making the trench dug a moderate distance from the river, and threw the earth toward the camp; and the Babylonians laughed at the siege, as having provisions for more than twenty years. When the trench was dug, Cyrus, watching for a night on which he knew the Babylonians would keep a feast, drinking and reveling the whole night, on this gathered a multitude and opened the trenches to the river—this is the Euphrates, as Herodotus relates; and the water passed into the trenches in the night, and the channel of the river through the city became passable for men, the water being diverted. Then, sending down into the dry bed of the river attendants and foot and horse, he ordered them to see whether it was passable. Meanwhile, conversing with the leaders of the multitude and rousing them to the work, at last he said, "Come, take up your arms; I will lead; and do you, Gobryas and Gadatas, show the ways, knowing them. And when we are within, lead with all speed to the palace." Upon this they went. And going as quickly as they could, those with Gobryas and Gadatas came to the palace, and found the gates shut, and fell upon the guards as they drank. When a cry and tumult arose, those within, the king having ordered them to see what the matter was, opened the gates, into which the enemy fell and came to the king. And they found him already standing and drawing the scimitar he had. And him those with Gadatas and Gobryas overpowered, and those with him died, some defending themselves, some giving way. And Cyrus sent the squadrons of horse through the streets, having proclaimed that whomever they took outside they should kill, but should proclaim to those in the houses, those who knew how to speak Syriac, to remain within, and that if anyone were caught outside, he would die. Meanwhile Gobryas and Gadatas came, and because they had avenged themselves on the unholy king, first they worshipped the gods, then kissed Cyrus's hands and feet.

Xenophon, relating the affairs of Cyrus, does not give the name of the captured king of the Assyrians; but Josephus, in the tenth book of the Antiquities, records that this was that Baltasar to whom also the hand appeared coming forth from the wall and writing the letters already mentioned, whose interpretation Daniel explained.

25. When day came, the holders of the citadel, perceiving that the city was taken and their king dead, surrendered the citadel too. And Cyrus sent into them commanders and guards. Then, calling the magi, since the city was spear-won, he ordered firstfruits to be set apart for the gods, and he distributed houses and public buildings to those who had shared in his deeds; and for himself he intended to prepare a manner of living befitting a king. But that he might not become an object of envy to his friends, he wished to do this with their consent, and conversing with them, by what he said he persuaded them to ask for this. From there he enters the palace, and sets guards about himself, and those who tended his person he gelded and made eunuchs, and chose for bodyguards Persians to the number of ten thousand, and in the city he posted sufficient guards. Having done this, he trained the more honoured of the army not to live without toil and in luxury; and over other matters he set other overseers—receivers of revenues, I mean, and dispensers of expenditures, superintendents of works and guardians of possessions, and overseers of provisions for living, and managers of horses and dogs; but those whom he thought should be guardians of his prosperity, the care of these he assigned to himself. And since to benefit men with money was added to him, he knew that no benefit is more pleasing to men than the giving of food and drink; therefore he ordered much to be set before him like what he himself ate, and enough for very many, and what was set out, except what he and his fellow-diners used, he distributed. And he became the most generous of men. But to surpass in the greatness of gifts, being the richest, is no marvel; but to surpass, while a king, in the care and attention to friends, this is more noteworthy. And a saying of his is remembered, that the works of a good herdsman and of a king are alike; for he said the herdsman should use his beasts after making them well-fed, and the king likewise should use cities and men after making them prosperous.

It is said too that Croesus once said to him that by giving much he would become poor, and was asked by Cyrus, "How much money do you think I would now have, if I had been collecting gold as you bid since I have been in the rule?" And Croesus said some large number. And Cyrus said, "Come now, Croesus, send a man with this Hystaspes. And you, Hystaspes, going round to the friends, tell them that I need money for a certain undertaking, and bid them, each as much as he can, provide me money, and writing it and sealing it, give the letters to Croesus's servant." And writing and sealing all that he charged Hystaspes, he gave it to him to carry to the friends. And he wrote to all to receive Hystaspes as his friend. When he had gone round and Croesus's servant had brought the letters, Hystaspes said, "Cyrus, king, use me now too as a rich man; for I am present with very many gifts because of your letters." And Cyrus said, "Here is one treasury for us, then, Croesus; but survey the others, and reckon how much ready money I have, if I need to use any." It is said that Croesus, reckoning, found many times more than he had said would be in the treasuries for Cyrus if he had been collecting; and upon this Cyrus said, "You see, Croesus, that I too have treasures."

It having seemed good to him to make a procession to the precincts set apart for the gods, calling those who held office among the Persians and the rest, he distributed to them Median robes; and then first the Persians put on the Median robe. When he had distributed the finest robes to the best men, he brought out other Median robes too—for he had prepared very many, sparing neither purple nor dark nor scarlet nor crimson garments—and apportioning to each of the leaders a part of them, he ordered them to adorn their subordinates with these. And one of those present asked him, "And you, Cyrus, when will you adorn yourself?" And he said, "Do I not seem to you now to be adorning myself, while adorning you? For if I can do good to my friends, in whatever robe I am, in that I shall appear fair." Having made the procession and sacrificed to the gods, he dined with his friends, seating those whom he most honoured at his left hand, as being more open to plot against than the right, and the rest at his right. After supper he sent home those who had allied with him as volunteers, except those who wished to remain with him; to these he gave land and houses. And to those who departed, both soldiers and officers, he gave many gifts. Then to the soldiers and officers about him he distributed all the money he had taken from Sardis according to each one's worth. And when they had received what was given, they said of Cyrus, "Surely he himself has much, since he has given so much to each of us too." But others said, "It is not Cyrus's way to amass money, but he delights more in giving than in getting." Perceiving this, Cyrus gathered his friends and all the men of standing and said, "It seems to me a mark of the simplest character for the ruler, having made his power manifest, to contend on the basis of it for nobility. And I, then," he said, "wish to show you all that I have that can be seen, and what cannot be seen, to describe." Saying this, he showed much fair money, and described what was so stored as not to be easily seen. And he said, "Men, you must consider these no more mine than yours; for I gather these that I may have something to give to whoever of you does any fair thing, and that, if any of you needs anything, he may take it by coming to me."

26. When he had set the affairs in Babylon in good order, he made ready to go off to Persia. And as, journeying, he came to Media, Cyrus turned to Cyaxares, and greeting him said that a house had been chosen for him in Babylon, and gave him many fair gifts. And Cyaxares sent to him his daughter, bringing a golden crown and bracelets and a necklace and a most beautiful Median robe. And the girl crowned Cyrus, and Cyaxares said, "I give you, Cyrus, this very woman to wife, being my daughter, and I give with her as dowry all Media; for I have no legitimate male child." And Cyrus said, "The lineage, Cyaxares, I commend, and the girl and the gifts, but I wish to marry her with the consent of my father and mother." And saying this he journeyed to Persia. Coming to the borders of the Persians, he left the army there, and himself with his friends entered the city, bringing victims enough for all the Persians to sacrifice and feast. He brought gifts for his father and mother such as was fitting, and for his friends such as befitted magistrates and elders; and he gave to all Persians, and indeed to Persian women too. And having spent some time with his parents, he departed. And coming to Media, with his father's consent he married the daughter of Cyaxares; and having married, at once taking her with him he set out.

When he came to Babylon, he sent satraps to the subdued nations—to Arabia, that is, and Cappadocia, to Greater Phrygia, to Lycia and Ionia, to Caria, to Phrygia by the Hellespont and Aeolis. To the Cilicians and Cyprians and Paphlagonians he did not send satraps, because they seemed to march with him willingly; yet these too paid tribute. And that, his rule being great, reports might be conveyed to him quickly even from afar, he considered how long a road a horse driven hard could accomplish, and he made horse-stations so far apart from one another, and set horses in them and those who cared for them, and posted at each a suitable man to receive the dispatches conveyed and to deliver them, and to take the worn-out horses and send others fresh.

When a year had now passed he made a campaign, in which he is said to have subdued all the nations that dwell from where one enters Syria as far as the Red Sea. After this he marches against Egypt and subdues it too; so that from there his rule was bounded on the east by the Red Sea, on the north by the Euxine Sea, on the west by Cyprus and Egypt, and Ethiopia on the south. And he himself, making his abode in the midst of these, passed seven months in Babylon, the winter season, for this country is warm, three months about spring in Susa, and in Ecbatana two months he spent, the height of summer.

Having so lived, and being now very old, Cyrus comes to Persia for the seventh time, his parents having long since died. And as he slept in the palace, there seemed to him in a dream one greater than a man to come to him, saying, "Make ready, Cyrus; for now the gods summon you." From this he guessed that the end of his life was at hand, and on the third day he called his sons, for they accompanied him, and his friends and the rulers of the Persians, and said, "To me the end of life is now at hand, and I must make clear concerning the kingdom, to whom it shall belong after me, that it may not, becoming disputed, cause you trouble. You, then, Cambyses, being the elder, hold the kingdom, the gods granting and I; and to you, Tanaoxares, I give to be satrap of the Medes and Armenians and Cadusians." Having charged his sons with these things and exhorted them much, and having addressed those present and given his right hand to all, he covered himself and so departed. And when he was gone, at once his sons fell into faction, and cities and nations revolted, and all turned to the worse.

These things, then, are related by Xenophon concerning Cyrus; but Herodotus of Halicarnassus says other things about Cyrus's upbringing and end and the rest of his life, which it would be long to relate. And for me, who have made an epitome of history, it is not fitting to set down a work of many lines; but I myself have written the more probable things, and whoever wishes to know what Herodotus too wrote about him, taking up his book will find these things in the first book, to which he gave the title of the first of the Muses, Clio.

4.1. So Cyrus brought to an end the empire of the Assyrians. In the first year of his reign, which was the seventieth since the Hebrews had been carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon, he permitted the Jews in Babylon to depart to Jerusalem and to rebuild both the city and the temple, just as the prophet Jeremiah had foretold, and before him Isaiah had spoken of it. For Jeremiah lived at the time when the city was taken and the temple razed, while Isaiah lived a hundred and forty years before the city was captured and the temple destroyed. And Cyrus not only granted the captives their return and the raising up again of the city and the temple, but also sent back with them the vessels of the temple which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off to Babylon, handing them over to Mithridates his treasurer and to Zerubbabel to convey. He wrote also to the satraps in Syria to help them in the building of the works and to supply the whole cost from the royal funds. When Cyrus had so decreed, the leaders of the two tribes, of Judah and of Benjamin, together with the Levites and the priests, set out; but many remained in Babylon, unwilling to abandon their possessions. When they reached Jerusalem, all of Cyrus's officials assisted them in the building and worked together with them. Those who returned were forty-two thousand six hundred in number.

While they were already pressing forward with the building of the city and the temple, the surrounding nations, and above all the Cuthaeans, whom Shalmaneser had settled in Samaria when he carried the Israelites into captivity, out of envy first won over the satraps not to assist the Jews in the building. Then, when Cyrus had ended his life and Cambyses his son had succeeded to the kingdom, they wrote to Cambyses, slandering the Hebrews as a rebellious and ungovernable nation, and saying that, if they completed the city and the temple, they would neither pay tribute nor be subject. By writing these things and many more of the kind they persuaded him to forbid the rebuilding of the city and the temple; and the works were halted until the second year of the reign of Darius the son of Hystaspes, for nine years. For Cambyses, having reigned seven years and in that time having subdued Egypt, died at Damascus on his return, while the Magi made themselves masters of the kingdom. It is well to recount these matters too in summary.

Cambyses had a brother named, according to Xenophon, Tanaoxares, but according to Herodotus, Smerdis. While Cambyses was in Egypt, it seemed to him in his sleep that someone stood over him and said that Smerdis had sat upon the royal throne and touched the vault of heaven with his head. Fearing then for his kingdom, he at once sent Prexaspes to Susa to kill his brother secretly. And so Smerdis was destroyed; but Cambyses did not escape his destiny. For there were two Median brothers, called Magi, of whom one was named Cataziethes and the other Smerdis. This Smerdis shared with Smerdis the son of Cyrus not only his name but also his appearance. One of these two Cambyses had taken as the steward of his affairs. While Cambyses lingered in Egypt, Cataziethes, learning of the murder of Smerdis the son of Cyrus and that his death was known to few, planned to seize the kingdom; and he set his brother, who bore the name of Smerdis and had a great resemblance to him, upon the royal throne, not as his own blood-brother, but as the son of Cyrus and the brother of Cambyses. And he sent heralds everywhere to proclaim Smerdis the son of Cyrus as king. When Cambyses learned of this, he examined Prexaspes as one who had not carried out his command. But Prexaspes maintained that it was not his brother who had risen against him: "For I," he said, "as you commanded, killed and buried him." Cambyses therefore ordered the man who in the army was proclaiming that Smerdis the son of Cyrus reigned over the Persians to be arrested. When he was arrested, he was asked whether he himself had seen Smerdis, and whether Smerdis had ordered him to say what he was saying. He answered that he had not seen Smerdis, but that he had been ordered to say these things by the Magus who governed the palace. Learning the truth from this, Cambyses lamented that he had killed his brother in vain, and at once set out to march against the Magi. But as he leaped upon his horse, the cap fell from the scabbard of his sword, and the bared blade struck his thigh a mortal blow. He asked then what the city was called, and learning that it was Ecbatana, he said, "Here it is fated for me to die." For it had been prophesied to him that he would die at Ecbatana; and he had supposed that his end would overtake him at the Median Ecbatana, but the oracle meant not that place, but the Syrian Ecbatana. So a few days later he died childless,

4.2. having reigned seven years and five months. And the Magus, when Cambyses was dead, reigned without fear, ascribing to himself the name of Smerdis the son of Cyrus. He sent word to every nation he ruled and proclaimed remission of taxes for all for three years. But when he had reigned seven months, it became known who he was, and it became known in this way. Otanes was a man who rivalled the foremost of the Persians in birth and wealth. Cambyses had married his daughter, who was called Phaedymia; and the Magus made use of her, as of the other women whom he found in the palace. Her father, therefore, secretly sent and asked her whether she lay with Smerdis the son of Cyrus or with some other man. She answered that she had never seen Smerdis the son of Cyrus, and did not know with whom she shared a bed. Again he sent to her, charging her, if need be, to take the risk, in order to fulfil her father's command, and instructing her that, when she should lie with the king and find him asleep, she should feel for his ears; and if she found that he had ears, she should know that she lay with Smerdis the son of Cyrus, but if he had none, she should consider him to be the Magus Smerdis. Phaedymia obeyed her father, and finding that the man who lay with her had no ears, she made it known to her father. He had no ears because Cyrus had once cut them off for some offence. Then Otanes shared the secret with Aspathines and Gobryas, the foremost of the Persians and his friends. They, already suspecting the matter, at once accepted his words. They resolved to take in others as well. And Otanes brought in Intaphernes, Gobryas brought in Megabyzus, and Aspathines brought in Hydarnes; and to Darius the son of Hystaspes, who had just come to Susa from Persis, they communicated the secret. He too accepted the proposal, and advised them to set about the deed at once, saying that if the present day passed in vain, he himself would become the informer of the plot to the Magus. The others were persuaded by Darius's advice and held to the work.

Something else also occurred which spurred them to hasten the attempt. For the Magi, knowing that Prexaspes had with his own hand wrought the murder of Smerdis the son of Cyrus, and that for this reason he stood accused among the Persians, summoned him, made him their friend, and bound him beforehand with oaths and brilliant promises not to reveal their device to anyone. When he had agreed to do this, they went further and proposed that they would gather the multitude beneath the wall of the palace, and that he should climb upon a tower and cry out within hearing of all that they were ruled by Smerdis the son of Cyrus and by no other; for they had spared him, and had not killed him as Cambyses had commanded. When he had agreed to do this too, the multitude was gathered, and Prexaspes went up upon the tower and told of all the good that the Persians had received from Cyrus. But he added that he himself had killed Cyrus's son Smerdis, compelled by Cambyses, and declared plainly that it was the Magi who held the kingdom, and called down curses on the Persians if they did not avenge themselves on them. Having said this, he threw himself down and died.

The seven men, learning on the road what Prexaspes had done, hastened at once to the palace and entered it, unhindered by the guards, who stood in awe of the eminence of the men. Passing into the court, they met the eunuch messengers, who asked them on what errand they had come and tried to prevent them going further. They cut down the eunuchs on the spot and ran on inside. The Magi, who were within, learning of the tumult from the eunuchs, turned to defend themselves: one took up a spear, the other a bow. The one with the spear struck Aspathines in the thigh and Intaphernes in the face, whereby his eye was injured; but the bow proved useless to those who fought hand to hand at close quarters. The one who held it slipped into a chamber, and Darius and Gobryas burst in after him. Gobryas grappled with the Magus, while Darius, at a loss because of the darkness and afraid of striking his comrade, stood idle. Gobryas asked why he stood inactive; and he told the cause. "Then thrust your sword through both of us," said Gobryas. Darius drove in his dagger, and struck the Magus. So they killed both, and cut off the heads of both. The two wounded men they left in the citadel, both because of their wounds and to guard the acropolis; the rest, carrying the heads of the Magi, ran out and showed them to the Persians and explained what had happened. The Persians, learning of the deception, killed every Magus they met.

4.3. When the tumult had subsided and some days had passed, they took counsel about the management of affairs. Otanes urged them to choose a democracy, Megabyzus an aristocracy, but Darius advised that they choose a kingdom once again. The other four agreed with his opinion; and they resolved to mount their horses, and that whoever's horse, when they had come into the suburb, should neigh first at sunrise, he should hold the kingdom. Darius explained the plan to his groom. The man was clever, and "Take courage, master," he said, "for the kingdom shall be yours." When night came, he took a mare which Darius's horse loved, and tying it in the suburb he led the horse there and walked it close to the mare, and at last let it cover her. At dawn, when the seven had come into the suburb and were riding through it, as soon as they reached the place where the mare had been tied, Darius's horse, remembering her, went forward and neighed; and thereby the kingdom fell to Darius. Some say that it was Oebares — for that was the name of Darius's groom — who contrived this; but others say that his contrivance was different: that he touched with his hand the parts of the mare which Darius's horse loved, and kept his hand hidden in his trousers; and when the sun was rising and the seven men were mounting their horses, he brought his hand to the nostrils of Darius's horse, and the horse, at once catching the scent, snorted and neighed. Whether it happened in the one way or the other, Darius obtained the kingdom.

This man, while still a private person, had vowed to God that, if he became king, he would send to the temple in Jerusalem all the vessels of God that were still in Babylon. He had also long had a friendship with Zerubbabel, on account of which Zerubbabel, having lately come to him from Jerusalem, had been thought worthy to serve among his bodyguards together with two others. In the first year of his reign Darius prepared a banquet for his nobles; and when they had feasted and departed, he himself fell asleep beside his couch. Having slept a little, he woke and conversed with his bodyguards. He set each of them a contest of speech: to the first, whether wine prevails over all things; to the second, whether kings do; and to the remaining one — this was Zerubbabel — whether women, and above them truth, prevail. And he promised to give the victor as a prize to wear purple, and a turban of fine linen, and a golden collar, and to drink from golden cups, and to sleep upon gold, and to have a chariot with a golden bridle, and to sit next after himself, and to be called his kinsman. At dawn, then, summoning the nobles, he bade each of the bodyguards declare his opinion on the question. The first extolled the strength of wine, as deceiving the mind of those who indulge in it, altering the dispositions of their souls, and making the drunken now this, now that. The second argued that the king prevails over all, since men, ruling all other things through wisdom, are themselves ruled by kings, to whom all things are subject. But Zerubbabel declared that women are stronger, since kings and those who plant the vines are born of women, and all men honour them above their parents and their homelands and their dearest; and even kings themselves are mastered by women, flattering them and humbling themselves if they perceive them displeased in anything. But truth, he said, is stronger than all these; for God too is true and is so called, and while all else is mortal, truth is an immortal thing and everlasting. When all judged that he had argued best concerning truth, Darius granted him to ask whatever he wished beyond what had been promised. And he reminded Darius of the vow which he had made, if he should obtain the kingdom. This was, to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, and to restore all the vessels that still remained in Babylon. "This," he said, "is my request." The king, pleased at this, wrote to the satraps to supply cedar timber for the building of the temple, and to help Zerubbabel build the city, and that all the captives of the Israelites who had gone away to Judaea should be free and exempt from tribute, and that fifty talents should be given for the raising of the temple. And he sent all the vessels that were still with him; and whatever Cyrus had decreed concerning the Jews, this Darius too ordained in addition.

4.4. When these things had been done, Zerubbabel came to Babylon and announced to his countrymen the king's good tidings; and all who were eager to return to Jerusalem departed. The sum of those who went away was four million six hundred and twenty-eight thousand, apart from the Levites and gatekeepers and temple servants and attendants who followed those going up. Their leader was Zerubbabel, son of Salathiel, of the tribe of Judah, a descendant of David, and Jesus the son of Josedek the high priest; and besides these, Mardochaeus and Sereb were appointed as leaders from among the multitude. Having gone away to Jerusalem, they offered sacrifice and began the building of the temple. The temple was soon completed; and when the sanctuary was finished, the priests and the Levites and the sons of Asaph sang hymns to God. But the elders of the families, recalling the former temple in their memories and seeing that the one now built was inferior to the old, were moved to tears and lamentation, and their wailing drowned out the sound of the trumpets.

The Samaritans came to Zerubbabel while the temple was still being raised, asking to share with them in the building of the temple. But he did not allow them to share in the building, though he said they were permitted to worship in the temple. At this the Samaritans were aggrieved, and they persuaded the nations in Syria to ask the satraps to halt the raising of the temple. The governors of Syria and Phoenicia went up to Jerusalem and asked by whose leave they were raising the temple like a fortress and surrounding the city with walls exceedingly strong. Zerubbabel and the high priest Jesus said that the building had first been permitted by Cyrus, and then again by Darius. The governors of the lands of Syria and Phoenicia did not decide to halt the building of the works, but wrote at once to Darius. The Jews, fearing lest the king should change his mind about what he had ordained, were urged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah to take courage and to fear nothing untoward. Trusting therefore in the prophets, they pressed on intently with the building. Darius, on receiving the letters and the accusations of the Samaritans — that the Jews were fortifying the city and building the temple like a fortress, and that Cambyses had forbidden their building — ordered that the matter be searched out in the royal records. And it was found written at Ecbatana, the fortress in Media, that in the first year of his reign Cyrus had commanded the temple in Jerusalem and the altar to be built, and had ordained that the expense for these should come from the royal funds, and that the vessels of the temple should be restored, and had commanded the rulers there to help with the work and to supply the Jews for sacrifice with bulls and rams and lambs and kids, and fine flour and wine and oil. Finding these things in the records, Darius wrote back to those who had written to him: "I have sent you the copy of the letter which I found in the records of Cyrus, and it is my will that all be done as it contains. Farewell." When the governors of those lands learned the king's purpose, they worked together with the Jews. And the temple was built in seven years, and the Israelites offered sacrifices of renewal for the good things of former times. When the feast of unleavened bread came, all the people streamed together from the villages into the city, and they kept the feast and accomplished the sacrifice called the Passover.

They settled in Jerusalem, employing an aristocratic government tempered with oligarchy. For the priests presided over affairs until it came about that the descendants of Asamonaeus reigned. Before the captivity they had been ruled by kings for five hundred and thirty-two years, six months, and ten days; and before the kings, those called judges and monarchs governed them as rulers. And living under this form of government they passed more than five hundred years after Moses and Joshua.

But the Samaritans, being hostile toward them, did the Jews many injuries. Envoys, therefore, were sent from Jerusalem to Darius — Zerubbabel and four others of the rulers. When the king learned the charges against the Samaritans, he wrote to the commanders and the council of Samaria not to trouble the Jews in any way, but rather to supply them from the royal treasury, out of the revenue of Samaria, with all things useful to them for sacrifice.

4.5. When Darius died, his son Xerxes succeeded to the kingdom and inherited also his piety toward God, and he behaved most generously toward the Jews. There was at that time in Babylon Ezra, a good man and most exactly versed in the laws of Moses. He became a friend of Xerxes, and wishing to go up to Jerusalem and to take with him some of the Hebrews in Babylon, he asked the king to make him known to the satraps by his letters. And the king wrote thus: "Considering it a work of my own benevolence that those of the Israelites who wish should depart with him to Jerusalem, I have given this command to Ezra, priest and reader of the divine law; and let whoever wishes depart. And whatever silver and gold may be found in the land of the Babylonians that has been dedicated to God, I command that all of it be conveyed to Jerusalem. And whatever you may devise, O Ezra, this also do, making the expense for it out of the royal treasury. And I command that on the priests and Levites and all the servants of the temple no tribute nor any other burden be imposed. And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of God, appoint judges, that they may give judgment throughout all Syria and Phoenicia, men who know the law; and to those who do not know it you shall grant the means of learning it." When Ezra had received this letter, he read it in Babylon to the Jews there, and sent a copy of it to all his countrymen; and they all rejoiced greatly. Many of them took up their possessions and came to Babylon, that they might return to Jerusalem; but the whole body of the Israelites remained in their place. Therefore Josephus says that two tribes in Asia and in Europe were subject to the Romans, but that the ten tribes were beyond the Euphrates, being countless myriads and not able to be reckoned by number. Many in number came to Ezra and went up with him to Jerusalem. And Ezra handed over to the treasurers what Xerxes and his counsellors and the Israelites in Babylon had given to God, amounting to many talents of silver and bronze, and delivered the king's letters to the governors of the lands. They honoured the nation and helped them in every need. Then, learning that some of the people and of the priests and Levites had married foreign wives, he persuaded them, with many tears and frequent exhortations, to put away the foreign wives and the children born of them. When the feast of Tabernacles came, nearly the whole multitude of the people gathered together for it, and they asked Ezra that the laws of Moses be read. Hearing them, they were moved to tears, grieving over the past. But Ezra said that they ought not to lament during a feast, but to keep festival and to feast and to observe the laws in time to come.

So Ezra died an old man; and one of the captives, Nehemiah by name, who was cup-bearer to Xerxes, while walking before Susa saw certain strangers entering the city, and hearing them speaking in Hebrew, he approached and asked whence they came. When they said they had come from Jerusalem, he asked further how the multitude and the mother-city Jerusalem fared. When they answered that they fared ill, for the surrounding nations brought many terrible things upon them, Nehemiah wept; and when the hour came, he went in to serve the king as he was. The king, seeing him downcast, asked why he was dejected. He told that the cause of his grief was the misfortunes of his homeland, and begged that he might be allowed to go and raise up the wall and complete what was lacking of the sanctuary. The king assented to the request, and the next day gave him a letter to the governor of Phoenicia and Syria and Samaria, charging him to honour Nehemiah and to supply the expense for the building. So Nehemiah came to Jerusalem, with many of his countrymen following him, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of Xerxes, and delivered the letter to the governor of the said lands. He distributed the building of the wall among the people by villages and cities, that it might be finished as quickly as possible. And the Jews prepared themselves for the work — so called from the day when they went up from Babylon, for since the tribe of Judah came first to those places, both the people themselves and the land alike were renamed from them as Jews. But the Ammonites and Moabites and Samaritans were vexed at the building of the walls, and attacked them and slew very many, and plotted against Nehemiah himself. And the multitude, thrown into disorder by these things, almost gave up the building. But Nehemiah, setting a body of men to guard his person, persevered unwearied, going around the circuit of the city by night and day; and this hardship he endured for two years and four months. For in that time the wall of Jerusalem was completed, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of Xerxes, in the ninth month. Nehemiah, seeing the city short of inhabitants, urged the priests and Levites to leave the countryside and move into the city. Nehemiah died an old man, a man honest in character and just and most generous toward his countrymen.

4.6. When Xerxes died, the kingdom passed to his son Cyrus, whom they also call Artaxerxes. In the third year of his reign he summoned the governors and satraps of his subject nations and feasted them lavishly for many days; and the queen Vashti likewise held a banquet for the women. Since she surpassed all in beauty, the king wished to display her to those banqueting with him, and he sent and bade her come to the banquet. But she would not obey; and though he sent often, she remained unyielding. The king therefore was angered at her disobedience. And he communicated her disobedience to the seven counsellors of the Persians; and they judged that she must be cast out. So she was cast out; but the king grieved, for he was in love with her. To him in this state his friends advised that he gather fair maidens from everywhere and take as wife the one judged most worthy.

He was persuaded by this advice, and when many maidens had been assembled, there was found in Babylon a certain Jewish maiden by birth, of the tribe of Benjamin, orphaned of both parents and reared by her uncle Mardochaeus, one of the foremost among the Jews. Esther was the maiden's name. The king, delighted with her, took her to wife and set the diadem upon her. And her uncle moved from Babylon to Susa, spending his time about the palace and inquiring after his niece. For neither did she make plain the nation from which she came, nor did Mardochaeus acknowledge his kinship with her. The king had made a law that no one might approach him while he sat upon his throne unless summoned, or else the one so approaching would die at the hands of the axe-bearers who stood by him, unless he held out toward him the rod which he kept in his hand; for whoever touched the rod was safe. When two of his eunuchs plotted against the king Artaxerxes, Barnabazus, a servant of one of them, a Jew by birth, perceiving the plot, reported it to Mardochaeus, who through Esther disclosed the conspirators to the king. The king crucified the eunuchs, and ordered the name of Mardochaeus to be written in the records and that he should remain at the palace.

Now Haman, being a particular friend of the king, was reverenced by all. But when Mardochaeus did not reverence him on account of his law, Haman, learning that he was a Jew, was indignant and said to him that, while the free Persians reverenced him, he, being a slave, refused to do so. Coming therefore to the king, he accused the whole nation, and asked that he order it to be destroyed root and branch and that no remnant of it be left; and that the king might not be deprived of their tribute, he himself undertook to give four hundred thousand pieces of silver. So Haman asked these things; but the king both made him a gift of the silver and gave him the people, to do with them as he wished. At once, then, a decree was sent by Haman to all the nations as if from the king, containing this: "Those designated by my second father Haman I command all to be destroyed, with their wives and children, and I will this to be done on the fourteenth of the twelfth month of the present year." When this letter was carried to the cities and the lands, the destruction of the Jews was being prepared. And those in Susa were in the same case.

When Mardochaeus learned what had happened, he put on sackcloth and poured ashes upon himself and cried aloud that a nation that had done no wrong was being destroyed. Coming to the palace, he stood outside; for it was not permitted to enter in such a garb. When Esther the queen learned of this, she sent a eunuch to Mardochaeus to learn why he mourned; and he made known to the eunuch what had happened, and charged Esther to entreat the king concerning these things. But she, learning this, sent word to him that, unless summoned by the king, she feared she would die if she came to him unsummoned. Mardochaeus replied that she should not look to her own safety, but to that of the nation; and that, if she did not, help would by all means come to it from God, but she and her father's house would be destroyed. She then charged him to go to Susa and prepare the Jews there to fast three days for her sake. Mardochaeus did so; and Esther, casting herself upon the ground in mourning garb and remaining without food for three days, prayed to God. After the three days she put on royal attire and, with two handmaids — on one of whom she leaned lightly, while the other bore up with her fingertips the deep folds of her robe that flowed even to the ground — she came to the king and entered with fear. When she came before him as he sat in royal state upon the throne, and he looked upon her sternly, a faintness seized her from fear, and she fell senseless upon the maid who walked at her side. But the king, fearing for the woman — God so providing it — leaped up from the throne, and taking her in his arms revived her, kissing her and bidding her take courage, and stretching out toward her his golden staff and placing the sceptre in her hands. She, taking heart from this, asked him to come to a banquet, together with Haman, with her. When he had assented and they were present, the king bade her declare what she wished, for she would fail of nothing. But she said she would tell him her wish on the morrow, if he would come again to her at a banquet together with Haman. When the king had promised, Haman went out full of joy; and seeing Mardochaeus in the court, he was indignant that he did not reverence him. Coming home to his wife and friends, he told of the honour he enjoyed both at home and from the queen, and how it grieved him to see Mardochaeus in the court. His wife bade him have a stake of fifty cubits cut, and in the morning to ask the king for leave to crucify Mardochaeus. Approving the counsel, he ordered his servants to prepare a stake and set it up in the court for the punishment of Mardochaeus.

And the stake was ready; but God that night took away the king's sleep. Lying awake, he ordered the secretary to bring the records of his own deeds and to read them. As they were being read, it was found that Mardochaeus had become the king's informer concerning the plot of the eunuchs. When the secretary had told only this and was passing on to another deed, the king stopped him, asking whether there was recorded any reward given to Mardochaeus. When he heard that there was none, he asked what hour of the night it was; and learning that it was already dawn, he commanded that whichever of his friends they found before the court should be called in. Haman was found, having hastened to ask for Mardochaeus. When he was summoned, the king said to him, "Advise me how I might honour a man who is loved by me." Reckoning that whatever opinion he gave he would be giving on his own behalf — for he supposed himself loved by the king more than the rest — he said, "If you wish to glorify this man, set him upon a horse, wearing the same attire as yourself and bearing a golden collar, and let one of your most intimate friends go before him and proclaim throughout the whole city that he obtains this honour whom the king wishes to honour." Pleased with the advice, the king said, "Seek out Mardochaeus the Jew, and giving him the horse and the robe and the collar, go before him and make the proclamation yourself; for you are my most intimate friend. These things shall be his from me, for he saved my life." Hearing this, Haman was confounded, and though stricken with helplessness, he nevertheless went out, leading the horse and bearing the purple and the collar. Finding Mardochaeus before the court clad in sackcloth, he bade him put on the purple. But he said, "Most wicked of men, do you thus mock our misfortunes?" When he learned, however, that the king had granted him this as a reward instead of death, for revealing the plot of the eunuchs, he put on the purple and the collar, and mounting the horse he rode around the city, with Haman going before and proclaiming that thus the king honours whomever he loves.
So when Haman had gone around the city, he returned to the king;

4.7. and Haman went home and recounted to his wife, weeping, what had befallen him. While they spoke, there came from Esther eunuchs urging Haman to hasten to the dinner. One of these, seeing the stake in his house and learning from one of the servants that they had prepared it to ask for the punishment of Mardochaeus, departed for the moment. When the banquet was drawing to its close, the king bade the queen say whom she begged for. She lamented the danger of her people, and said that she too, together with her nation, had been given over to destruction, and that it was Haman who had moved to ask for this. The king, troubled at this, sprang up from the banquet; and Haman entreated Esther, falling upon the couch and supplicating the queen. As the king came back in, "Most wicked man," he said, "do you also attempt to violate my wife?" At this moment the eunuch who was present spoke of the stake that he had seen prepared for Mardochaeus. And the king at once ordered that Haman be hanged upon that very stake. So he perished, and the queen received his property as a gift. When the king learned the kinship of Mardochaeus with Esther, he gave him the ring which he had formerly given to Haman. And the queen gave the property to Mardochaeus, and begged the king to deliver the nation of the Hebrews from danger. He granted leave to write in his name whatever they wished concerning the nation. And what was written was as follows. They accused Haman as wicked and ungrateful, who had asked for the destruction of a nation that had done no wrong, but they called Mardochaeus the saviour, and the Jews men who lived in the best manner and reverenced God; and they not only freed them from the punishment to which Haman had condemned them, but even thought them worthy of honour, and permitted them to live in peace using their own laws, and granted them on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, to defend themselves against those who had wronged them; and they ordered the satraps of the lands to help them, that they might take vengeance on their enemies.

When the Jews in Susa learned of the affair of Mardochaeus, they considered the good fortune common to all; and on the thirteenth of the month Adar, which the Macedonians call Dystros, the Jews in Susa killed about five hundred of their enemies, and those in the other cities and lands destroyed seventy-five thousand. Those in Susa, on the following day also, destroyed three hundred more, at Esther's request; and the ten sons of Haman were crucified, the king granting her this too. The fourteenth of the month the whole nation made a festival. And from that time they keep both days as a festival, calling them Days of Defence. And Mardochaeus was great, and helped the king govern the realm.

When the high priesthood passed to Joannes the son of Jodae, his brother Jesus, being a friend of Bagoas the general of the army of Artaxerxes, received a promise of obtaining the high priesthood. For this reason Joannes, provoked, killed his brother in the temple. And Bagoas, coming at once upon the temple, entered it, saying, "If those who have dared murder in the temple may enter it, I too will enter, being purer than they." And for seven years he afflicted the Jews. When Joannes ended his life, his son Joad succeeded to the high priesthood. He too had a brother, Manasses, to whom Sanaballetes, a satrap of Darius the last king of the Persians, gave his daughter, named Nicaso, in marriage. The leading men of the people of Jerusalem were in an uproar, because the brother of the high priest had married a foreigner, and ordered him either to divorce her or to abstain from the altar. He came to his father-in-law and told him this. Sanaballetes promised both to preserve his priesthood and to make him high priest and governor of the places he himself ruled, if he would not part from his daughter, and to build a temple on Mount Garizin, the highest of the mountains about Samaria, greater than the one in Jerusalem, with the consent of king Darius. Elated by these things, Manasses remained with Sanaballetes. And since many other priests and Israelites were entangled in such marriages, they all gathered to Manasses. Sanaballetes was preparing to bring his request concerning the building of the temple on Garizin to king Darius; but Darius, having engaged Alexander at Issus in Cilicia and being defeated, fled. Despairing then of Darius, Sanaballetes went over to Alexander with eight thousand of his men, and said that he handed over himself and the places he ruled to him. When Alexander received him, being now confident concerning his son-in-law, he brought his request for the raising of the temple on Garizin. And being permitted the building, he built the temple with all haste, and appointed Manasses his son-in-law high priest.

4.8. Since the course of the history has made mention of Alexander, it is well to recount briefly his deeds and his character, and from whence and of whom he sprang, and so to bring the account back again to its continuity; and the more so because this king visited Jerusalem, and something worthy of wonder happened from him toward the high priest and the people, and he himself recounted a certain divine vision, as Josephus records — which the account, as it proceeds, will set forth after the history concerning him.

He was the son of Philip the king of the Macedonians, born to him of Olympias; though it is told in fable that he was the son of Ammon, who lay with Olympias in the form of a serpent — and they say that Ammon is Zeus. But this is a fable. It is said, however, that his mother, on the night before she lay with Philip, dreamed that a thunderbolt fell upon her womb, and that from it a great fire blazed up and, carried in every direction, was dispersed. And after the marriage Philip dreamed that he set a seal upon his wife's womb, and that a lion was engraved on the seal. The other seers interpreted the dream variously, but Aristander said that she who had been sealed was with child — for empty things are not sealed — and that the child to be born would prove spirited and lion-like. He was born on the very day on which the temple of Artemis in Ephesus was burned down; when certain Magi present there ran about, saying that on that day there had been born for Asia a great ruin and grievous calamity.

Alexander was white of complexion, and the whiteness flushed red especially about his chest and face, and a sweet odour breathed from his skin and from his mouth.
